items.title: TikTok Hobby Seekers Find Escapism in the World of Miniatures
body: My first night at miniatures school, I dream about my childhood home. Not as it is now, with its empty-nester upgrades, but as it was when I was little. The kitchen floor tiles are still stars, laid down by my dad. My bedroom ceiling is sponge-painted with a sky. The back wall is missing, like a dollhouse. Everything is small — 1/12th of its normal size, the standard ratio for miniatures, where 1 inch equals 1 foot. No one is inside.
The second night of miniature school, I dream about grapes. I really need to make more grapes.

Called “minitopia” or “summer camp for miniaturists,” the annual communion of artists who make tiny things, officially known as Guild School, is the premier event on the miniature circuit. Each June the world’s greatest miniaturists come to the Maine Maritime Academy campus in the tiny coastal town of Castine to teach tricks and techniques to eager students. Guild School is run by the  International Guild of Miniature Artisans (IGMA), an industry body, with the motto “Making the world smaller.”

For one week students take courses on subjects such as thimble-size pottery and micro-crocheting using hooks the width of a sewing needle. I enroll in a class to make a cheese board the width of a silver dollar. Every day we use polymer clay to shape miniature Parmesan cheese rounds that crumble and flake like real Reggiano and bunches of grapes that seem so juicy they could pop.

To the uninitiated, the 1/12th scale doesn’t sound so small. But that’s 1/12th in three dimensions, 1,728 times smaller by volume. Grapes are petite; miniature grapes are the size of poppy seeds. “That is the right size … for Barbie,” says my teacher, Anna Wybranowska, of my first attempt. Barbie, at 1/6th scale, is looked down on in the miniatures community. I slice a grape in half with a razor. “Good.” She claps, delighted. “Now make 14,850 more.”

Most miniature objects are household items rendered small and then staged in boxes, cabinets or small houses (aka dollhouses). As a result, miniaturists are often stigmatized by those outside the art as adults who play with children’s toys.

“When you tell someone that you’re a miniaturist, you see two things,” says Carol Ward, an interior designer from Pittsburgh. We meet on our first night, in remedial Parmesan class. “People are either open and curious, or they lose respect for you immediately,” she says. “Especially men.”

For students, Guild School provides escape from a world that judges miniatures as frivolous or, worse, childish. Some are wary when they find out I’m a journalist. (Make sure you write that it’s a real art form, a woman from Texas admonishes me.) Being surrounded by adults obsessed with crafting miniatures creates a giddy, camplike atmosphere, complete with slightly grim cafeteria food salvaged by two-a-day ice creams. But the week is also serious, and a little bit dangerous, with hardcore power tools such as lathes and table saws.

IGMA’s style of miniature art isn’t simply making things that are small, but making them with the same precision and artistry one would aspire to in full size. It requires an exacting eye for detail and relentless perfectionism. In miniature the margin of error is smaller. Halfway through the week, a student is in despair at lunch: A single piece of sawdust trapped in her wood-carving jig has thrown off the balance of her entire miniature Hans J. Wegner easy chair.

Over the past few years, interest in miniatures has exploded, fueled by Instagram and TikTok, platforms that reward the awe-inducing precision miniaturists employ to make their objects. The art form has grown as a younger generation seeks analog hobbies in a digital era and innocent escapism in a world that increasingly feels out of control. Jumping on the trend, brands such as Sephora, Ikea, Arm & Hammer, Stila Cosmetics and Cath Kidston have all commissioned artists to create miniatures for social media promotions.

Guild School itself is small, and struggling to accommodate all who now want to come. The number of students attending for the first time was at an all-time high this year — 82 out of 232 overall, up from 68 new students out of 209 last year. Preregistration, which enters students in a lottery to choose their classes, sold out for the first time this summer. For 2027 it filled up in four hours.

Humans have made mini things for thousands of years, as offerings for tombs, teaching tools, currency and toys. There are countless examples from ancient Egypt and museums full of miniature models from Bronze Age civilizations in Crete, but they exist in every culture around the world. The 1/12th scale was formalized in the mid-16th century in continental Europe, when great dollhouses were crafted for European princesses, says Emily Wolverton, curator at the Mini Time Machine Museum of Miniatures in Tucson, Arizona. These finely wrought miniatures were not for play but for teaching the girls how to manage large households and staff.

Miniatures have ebbed and flowed in popular culture ever since. They tend to surge during times of rapid technological advancement, such as the 16th century Age of Exploration, when the world suddenly felt unfathomably large, and the Industrial Revolution, when the pace of human progress shifted into a new gear — and producing dollhouses became more affordable.

As teaching tools, miniatures can make a bigger world more accessible, offering glimpses into daily life across cultures and historical periods. During the Great Depression, very few Americans would ever visit Europe’s salons, visit Asia or see inside an immaculately designed Manhattan apartment. In 1930, Narcissa Niblack Thorne, a wealthy miniatures enthusiast from Chicago, began commissioning the creation of almost 70 room boxes from the top architects, designers and artists of the age to showcase historical as well as European, Asian and modernist interiors. Thorne’s miniature rooms traveled the country for a decade, allowing at least 1 million people to learn about design and inhabit spaces they would never walk through in real size.

At the time, Thorne’s miniature rooms were dismissed as decorative arts, the folly of a nostalgic heiress and an amateur, says Kit Maxwell, a curator at the Art Institute of Chicago, where the room boxes are exhibited. But the art world’s understanding of miniature art as fine art is shifting, a reconsideration that’s gaining momentum, Maxwell says. Thorne’s rooms are now considered masterpieces. “Imagination is a wonderful solace when the real world is hostile,” he says. Viewing the rooms, “you get the sense that there is benevolent human life.”

Miniatures were a popular hobby in the US in the 1970s, an era defined by stagflation, the Vietnam War and collapsing faith in institutions. But the hobby’s high barrier to entry and its aging demographic caused interest to wane as modern design took over in the ’80s.

Today “we are in an era of miniaturization again,” says Julie Steiner, one of the world’s top miniature knitters and senior director of admissions at the Barnes Foundation art museum in Philadelphia. “All of the world’s knowledge is shrunken into a device that fits in our pocket, and it’s overwhelming.”

Humans are hardwired to be attracted to, and physically stilled by, things that are small and cute. Staring at a finely wrought miniature thing — a chair, a hand-knotted rug, a peach layer cake — makes you feel wonder. It’s impossibly small, alarmingly real. The mind plays tricks. “By the very nature of it being small, you have to get close to it. You’re pulled in,” says Madeline Rislow, curator of the National Museum of Toys and Miniatures in Kansas City, Missouri.

When it comes to these miniature worlds, there are two distinct camps: dolls or no dolls, ever. When a space is vacant, it can be more easily inhabited by a viewer’s imagination. “If you put a doll in the room, it would look dead,” says Los Angeles-based cookbook author Lucy Lean, who discovered miniatures while renovating a house during the pandemic — it’s quicker, and cheaper, to test exuberant wallpaper in a tiny powder room.

Most doll-free miniature rooms are staged with the suggestion of action, even a little mess. There might be a blanket over the couch, food on the table or a coat hanging on a rack from someone who just slipped into the next room.

“People love miniatures because they can have the house in miniature they’ll never own in real life,” says Audrey Tripp, head of IGMA and the school’s ringmaster. “Some people are recreating places they’ve lost.”

Fiona Mah, a British museum exhibit designer who lives in Canada, began making miniatures as a hobby three years ago after seeing dollhouses on social media. She’d never had one as a child. She built one in the style of an English countryside cottage, a place she has happy memories of from growing up. She displays it in her (regular-size) house and posts pictures on Instagram. “I’m in Vancouver,” Mah says. “It’s a little piece of the nostalgic English countryside that doesn’t really exist. And I can control everything that goes in it and happens in it.”In Mah’s miniature house, there’s a book by the fire and a little bar of chocolate. “I suppose it’s me that lives in it,” she says.

Tuesday night is lobster dinner at Guild School, with cheap wine to loosen people up for the auction fundraiser following dessert. In the cafeteria, people wearing bibs kvetch about projects and progress. Lots of them have feelings about grapes. “I was sure I made 100 grapes,” says Amy Hsieh, a jewelry designer from Washington state. “I made 16.”

The students at Guild School range from hobbyists to Oscar-winning visual effects artists. The tuition cost for the vast majority of students ranges from $1,200 to $1,550 without accommodation or flights, plus $550 for daily lunch and dinner. Some save up for years to attend, whereas others think nothing of spending a few hundred dollars on a miniature bearskin rug at the auction. “It’s the most fiscally irresponsible thing I’ve ever done as an adult,” Mah says. “There are months where it’s like, can I buy groceries? And I’m just here making a miniature haberdashery cabinet.”

Most Guild School students are women. “If it was a sports week, no one would think twice about the cost. If it was something for men, if it was golf, it would be more expensive,” says Becky Gannon, a marketing consultant from Ohio who hosts Mad About Miniatures, a popular podcast.

The best miniatures can command jaw-dropping prices, often more than the regular-size item. Artists can’t just go to the store and buy the tools they need — often they have to make them first: single-hair paintbrushes, finger-length jigs and micro silicon molds. A single piece of furniture, a painting or a rug can require weeks of work.

At that night’s auction, most things sell for a few hundred dollars to a few thousand, depending on the artist. A tea table by artisan William R. Robertson sells in a bidding war to the soft-spoken Sheikh Ahmed bin Khalid Al-Thani of Qatar, a camp regular known for his classical taste and fierce bidding capacity, for $7,600.

Still, very few people who craft miniatures entirely by hand make much profit when the time and cost of labor is factored in. “Maybe you eke out minimum wage,” says hobbyist, collector and longtime Guild School student Barbara Kalty, who’s also a former IGMA president.

Most miniaturists both make and purchase pieces for their collections, with annual shows in Philadelphia, Chicago and London presenting the biggest buying opportunities. “People post videos of their hauls” on Instagram, says Steiner. “I was tallying in my head, and this collector has just shown, like, $30,000 in minis that they bought in a three-day period.”
Kalty, 82, estimates her doll and miniature collection is worth $250,000. Estate planning is a problem for many devoted miniaturists. “My daughter says, ‘I hope I die before you do,’ ” Kalty says.

Wednesday at Guild School is known as Weeping Wednesday. It marks the week’s halfway point, laying bare how much work remains before projects are presented on Friday night. There are whispers that a woman broke down crying in mini-pot-holder class.

I thought miniatures summer camp would be a chill assignment, but my time in Castine has the frenetic intensity of the first week of freshman year at university. You eat with new friends in the cafeteria before rushing to the next thing. People trade knowledge: There’s no such thing as an antique dollhouse that isn’t haunted; cinnamon is the best-looking rust; coffee grounds make great dirt, but you’ll get mice. Each night you collapse on your bed until your alarm goes off for your early-morning class. Your back hurts from hunching over workstations.
“It’s a lot of social intensity for this body of people,” Steiner says. “A lot of miniaturists are true introverts. We literally watch paint dry.”

Still, everyone wants to know if you’re having fun, if you’re planning to return next year. This is also practical; competition for accommodation is fierce. Hotels for the following year’s school are usually completely booked before camp ends.

“Last year my friend waited until Thursday to rebook, and there were no rooms left,” says Pattie Delekta. She and her sister paid the deposit for their 2027 room at the Castine Inn the day they arrived.

In the late 2010s it seemed entirely possible that skilled miniaturists would, quite literally, die out. The average age of people with the time and money to make miniatures was retirement. Attendance at both Guild School and the miniature shows was waning. The community resisted technology and social media.

Guild members were loath to accept more modern styles that were attractive to younger demographics. “There was a lot of Colonial and Victorian,” says Cathy Miller-Vaughan, owner of the Philadelphia Miniaturia, a popular annual miniature show. “In their minds it didn’t take as much work to create a bed that was copied from 1980 as opposed to 1872.”

When the pandemic canceled every miniature event in 2020, many worried it was the end. But people in lockdown with time on their hands began looking for creative outlets to both escape and feel some semblance of control. Some pulled out long-forgotten dollhouses from the attic or finally had time to learn to use the 3D printer they’d been given for the holidays. Miniature-focused accounts on social media racked up tens, then hundreds, of thousands of followers. Many new enthusiasts were unconstrained by traditional aesthetics, making furniture with 1970s flair or cottagecore fresh from Pinterest.

In the miniature circuit “it was the same people for years and years,” says Steiner, who sits on the IGMA board. “Now it’s all these people with pink hair and tattoos taking out their phones to photograph everything.”

This new generation discovered there was a limit to what they could learn online. “They just didn’t have the knowledge to step up their game,” Miller-Vaughan says. Those who find their way to Guild School learn that a 3D printer can’t replicate the errant details that sell a miniature to our imagination. An antique metal chair should be a bit tarnished; red grapes have a chalky exterior except for the few places where they’ve been buffed glossy (the trick is to use baby powder).

Still, younger students are less likely to be purists about technique. One, after telling me about her love for 3D printing stilettos for her miniature shoe closet, later asks me not to use her name in this story.

Regardless of how and when they came to the art form, what’s so gratifying for many miniaturists is the flow state they find working on something so small for so long. In a fast world, it slows you down. In the age of infinite scrolling, it holds your attention. Classroom time flies past. “Last night I was like, ‘Oh s---, I haven’t called my husband and son in two days,’ ” Mah says. She hopes to come back next year.

I get obsessed, sneaking back to my classroom in free periods to make more grapes. I’m not the only one. On Thursday after lunch, Linda Zechel almost amputates her finger in class making a wooden Windsor chair. That evening she’s bandaged and back in her class with Wybranowska. “Grapes don’t wait for anyone,” she says.

Miniatures demand a level of attention to the world around you. They force deep observation of the ordinary. To make something small is to understand its construction and to consider it from every angle. It’s knowing that a duck’s tail floats several inches off the water but that a duckling’s will be flush with the surface. That dust collects on one side of a box fan’s blades but not the other. Sometimes it means remembering in detail things, or places, that no longer exist.

Creating something in miniature “makes the mundane feel so beautiful and worthy of appreciation,” says Erica Meade, a miniaturist from the San Francisco Bay Area who works in the tech industry. She credits discovering the art form and making a dollhouse with curing her professional burnout. Meade made a miniature working box fan (complete with dust) that blew everyone’s minds and sold in the week’s silent auction for $2,301.

On Friday night, students present their projects in a show alongside their classmates. New and old friends make plans to see one another at coming miniature shows. I feel proud of my little cheese board but doubtful I’ll ever have the energy to undertake the herculean effort of filling a dollhouse. My friend Carol gives me a tiny wine glass, which I fill with red resin.

Tripp, the IGMA head, gives her closing remarks, thanking everyone for coming before breaking the painful news: “It’s time to return to the regular-sized world.” Afterward she looks me dead in the eye and, gesturing to what can only be described as all of Guild School, says, “Good luck making this miniature.”

items.title: SoftBank Raises Arm Margin Loan to $25 Billion as AI Bets Grow
body: SoftBank Group Corp. has increased its margin loan backed by shares of its chip unit Arm Holdings Plc by $5 billion to $25 billion, according to people familiar with the matter, as the conglomerate finds ways to fund its expanding investments in artificial intelligence.
The Japanese investment company renegotiated the terms and signed a deal with creditors this month, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private information.

It’s the third time SoftBank is upsizing its margin loan using Arm shares as founder Masayoshi Son needs billions of dollars to fund his growing AI investments, including a nearly $65 billion commitment to ChatGPT creator OpenAI.

SoftBank is among tech giants including Oracle Corp. and Meta Platforms Inc. that are pouring unprecedented amounts of capital into AI technologies and infrastructure. But investors are getting increasingly worried about the surge in Son’s multibillion-dollar AI projects where the revenue payoff is largely uncertain.
SoftBank declined to comment.

The margin loan — where a borrower uses investments like stocks as collateral — began as an $8.5 billion facility in 2023. It was subsequently increased to $13.5 billion in 2024 and then to $20 billion last year.
As of May, SoftBank’s loan was secured by 769 million shares of Arm, representing a 72% stake in the chip designer, according to company filings. SoftBank owns almost 90% of Arm.

SoftBank had drawn $20 billion from the facility as of December, with the loan set to expire in September 2027. The loan remains priced at an interest margin of about 225 basis points over the benchmark Secured Overnight Financing Rate and a credit adjustment spread of 25 basis points, some of the people said.

The deal drew strong demand, helped by the 142% spike in Arm’s share price this year. SoftBank was initially looking to increase the facility by $3 billion to $5 billion, but received about $7 billion in demand from lenders, the people said. SoftBank could boost the loan further if Arm shares continue to rise, they added.

SoftBank has been on an acquisition spree, led by its OpenAI investment. Other recent purchases include ABB Ltd.’s industrial robotics business for $5.4 billion and data center-focused private equity firm DigitalBridge Group Inc. for about $3 billion in cash.

To finance those deals, SoftBank has been replacing its shorter-term loans with debt carrying longer maturities to strengthen its financial position. SoftBank repaid this week the entire outstanding balance of $25.9 billion on a $40 billion one-year loan to fund its investment in OpenAI.

SoftBank also last month secured a $10 billion two-year loan using its OpenAI stake from lenders including Apollo Global Management Inc. Apollo is in talks with SoftBank about boosting the size of a loan to $9 billion from $5.4 billion to help the Japanese firm fund its OpenAI investment, Bloomberg reported this week.

Among tech giants, Oracle is considered to have one of the highest exposure to spending risk among the major AI players, which is overshadowing robust growth in its cloud-computing division. Meta’s capital expenditure has severely diminished its free cash flow, which is projected to turn negative in the third quarter.

For Son, his growing list of ambitions includes aggressive data center expansion in the US and France. SB Energy Inc., SoftBank’s US unit, is developing 8.8 gigawatts of data center capacity across America that is estimated to require $174 billion in capital spending. SoftBank has also announced plans to build a 5-gigawatt data center in France.

items.title: Turkey Turns to Two Big Banks to Liquidate Troubled Funds
body: Turkey has turned to two of its biggest banks to oversee the liquidation of 131 investment funds caught up in turmoil that has shaken the country’s asset-management industry.

Turkiye Is Bankasi AS and state-run Ziraat Bankasi AS will oversee the liquidation, the Capital Markets Board, or SPK, said in a statement late Thursday. The funds ordered into liquidation hold more than $18 billion in investments and have around 350,000 investors.
Isbank will handle funds established by Tera Portfoy Yonetimi AS, while Ziraat will oversee funds run by six other asset managers, including Pusula Portfoy Yonetimi AS.

The banks will sell assets held by the funds in stages and transfer the cash to investors in proportion to their holdings, according to the regulator. Redemption requests submitted after 1:30 p.m. on Sept. 17 will be given priority.

The move follows a week of turmoil in Turkey’s fund industry after funds at Tera and Pusula said they were unable to meet some investor redemption requests. The strains had been building since August, when regulators tightened rules on stock funds with concentrated holdings in companies with limited free floats, forcing some managers to unwind positions.

The stress then spilled into the wider market, driving a three-day selloff in Turkish stocks this week and sharp losses in scores of smaller shares. That prompted regulators and other authorities to step in with liquidations, trading bans and measures to ease liquidity. Authorities have also detained several finance executives, imposed travel bans and filed criminal complaints over alleged share-price manipulation.

items.title: Russians Fear Putin Will Send Them to War Once Election Is Over
body: Russians are growing fearful that President Vladimir Putin may soon order a massive new mobilization for the war in Ukraine after this weekend’s parliamentary elections.

That fear stretches to officials in the Kremlin and army recruitment centers, who’ve been looking to open foreign bank accounts and move assets abroad while encouraging friends and relatives to leave Russia in recent months, documents seen by Bloomberg News show.
While Putin denies he has any such plans, a European security official says Russia’s preparing to draft an additional 300,000 men into the army by the end of the year.

Unlike a previous mobilization in September 2022, which caused a spike in public anxiety and sent tens of thousands fleeing from Russia, there may be no formal announcement this time. That’s because the Kremlin has quietly built the digital infrastructure to summon people to the army while also closing off potential escape routes.

Three days of voting begin Friday in Russia’s first parliamentary elections since the start of the 2022 full-scale invasion. United Russia, which campaigns as the party of Putin, is expected to retain the majority in the State Duma that it has held since 2003 in the elections that are tightly controlled by the Kremlin.

Russia is incurring massive casualties for little progress on the battlefield in Ukraine, where Putin says he has about 700,000 troops deployed. The Kremlin needs to recruit about 400,000 people each year to replenish the army’s ranks and has relied mostly on offering huge recruitment bonuses and generous salaries to persuade people to sign military contracts. But with the war deep in its fifth year, there are signs the pool of volunteers is starting to dry up.

Russian regions recruited about 234,000 new contract troops between January and August, based on budget data, according to Janis Kluge, an analyst at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs in Berlin. That compares to about 260,000 in the same period last year, he wrote on Substack.

Russia is restructuring military commissariats to deal with increased flows of draftees, the European official said, asking not to be identified because the matter is sensitive. Advertising campaigns in Russia are urging men to sign military contracts to avoid the prospect of forced conscription.

Putin has called warnings of a post-election mobilization “complete nonsense” and part of a western information campaign against Russia. “From the point of view of the availability of military personnel, we have no problems here,” he said in Vladivostok on Sept. 3. “People are coming forward voluntarily and signing contracts.”

About 1,000 Russian soldiers are being killed in Ukraine each week in addition to those wounded, according to a person in Moscow familiar with situation. Russia needs more frontline troops and the quality of existing recruits is extremely low, the person said, asking not to be identified because the matter is sensitive.

Ukraine’s General Staff said Tuesday that 301,000 Russian troops had been killed and wounded so far this year, with monthly losses rising to 42,000 in July and August. It’s struggling with its own manpower challenges with about 1.5 million men on police wanted lists for evading conscription, and some 200,000 Ukrainian soldiers absent without leave.
Bloomberg News can’t independently verify the claims. Neither Russia nor Ukraine publishes official data on the numbers of their own troop casualties.

Putin continues to seek full control of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, where Russian forces are making grinding assaults to try to seize a fortress belt of cities they’ve failed to conquer in fighting since 2014. Ukraine rejects his demand to cede the territory as part of a deal to end the war.
Putin drew a direct connection between the election and the war in a televised address to the nation on Wednesday.
“Your choice and determination will show once again that millions of people are backing our fighters,” he said. “Participation in the elections is our joint contribution to Russia’s victory.”

Four other parties that are likely to gain seats in the parliamentary elections all support the war and there’s no genuine opposition. When the Yabloko party’s “for peace and freedom” campaign appeared popular enough to clear the 5% threshold for entry to the Duma, it was kicked off the ballot by Russia’s Supreme Court for supposed breaches of election rules.
What’s at Stake in Russia’s Wartime Duma Election?: Explainer

“Since the key issues are being resolved on the battlefield, the State Duma won’t be that important,” said Yevgeny Minchenko, a Moscow-based political scientist who’s worked with the Kremlin. “All the parties adhere to the presidential consensus.”

The Kremlin’s likely to focus mobilization efforts in the regions showing the greatest support for Putin in the elections, according to Ekaterina Schulmann, a Berlin-based political scientist at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center.

“In places where loyalty, discipline and administrative effectiveness were demonstrated, both by voters and by the authorities, more people could be recruited,” she said. “If they managed the elections well, they can also manage mobilization well in their region.”

European government officials say Putin has yet to make a final decision on mobilization. The negative public reaction to the call-up of 300,000 reservists in the 2022 draft remains etched in the memory of nervous Kremlin officials.

While that mobilization relied on serving paper notices to draftees, Russia’s digital Unified Military Register now automatically links with tax services, police databases, medical records, property registries, and border control.

Under updated regulations, an electronic summons is legally deemed to have been delivered seven days after it’s posted to the online portal regardless of whether the recipient opens it. An automatic exit ban takes effect at border posts as soon as the notice is published to prevent people leaving Russia.

For anyone failing to appear at a recruitment center within 20 days, automated penalties block access to public services including vehicle registration, real estate transactions, credit access, and self-employed business status.

Some officials worried that staffing reductions of up to 15% in Russia’s regions as part of budget cuts ordered by Putin earlier this year could result in those let go being called up to the front, the documents seen by Bloomberg indicate. There’s no sign the Kremlin currently has plans to do that, according to European government officials.

Still, rumors of an impending mobilization are stirring renewed anxiety, with reports of rising numbers of Russians crossing into neighboring countries such as Georgia and Armenia ahead of the elections. In August, Moscow accused Armenian officials of “provocative” statements after Yerevan indicated a readiness to welcome Russians fleeing military service.

Even as Putin insists his forces are advancing steadily in Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, Russia’s summer offensive yielded a gain of just 155 square kilometers (about 60 square miles) of territory from May to August, according to analysis by Alex Kokcharov, Bloomberg’s geoeconomic analyst for Russia, Eastern Europe and Central Asia. The analysis based on data compiled by DeepState, a Ukrainian open-source collective with links to the country’s military, compares to 2,037 square kilometers in the same period last year.

Russia’s army has sustained roughly 33,000 casualties on average per month so far this year for an average monthly gain of just 104 square kilometers, representing approximately 317 killed or wounded for every square kilometer taken, according to Kokcharov’s calculations.

“The military situation in recent months indicates that Russia does not have enough manpower both to concentrate forces on the main axis of advance and to reliably cover the front line,” said Kirill Rogov, head of Re: Russia, a Vienna-based research group. “In other words, mobilization would be necessary if the objective is to reach the borders of Donbas within six months.”

items.title: Merz Faces Down Party Revolt With Far Right Advancing in Germany
body: Friedrich Merz has been haunted by a past boast that he could cut the support of Germany’s surging far-right party in half.

Instead, the German chancellor watched this month as the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany trounced his conservative Christian Democrats in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. A satirical website quipped with a headline: “Merz Accidentally Halves Support for the Wrong Party.”

The fallout has shaken Germany’s political establishment and stoked calls within the party to push Merz out after only 16 months in office. With polls showing his personal popularity at a record low for any post-World War II chancellor, the crisis is set intensify on Sunday, when two more states head to the polls.

The turmoil has Merz — along with Germany’s political establishment — hobbled at a moment when Europe faces transatlantic tensions, a global energy crunch and China’s challenge on trade. Merz cancelled a trip to the United Nations next week to deal with the political storm in Berlin. During a flight to Finland for an Arctic security summit this week, he spent his time dialing party leaders to secure their backing, according to a person familiar with the situation.

Further losses loom in the Baltic coast state of Mecklenburg Western-Pomerania, where the party could especially face a thrashing, and the capital Berlin, where it risks falling behind the anti-capitalist Left party.

The chancellor has summoned the CDU leadership, including a powerful group of state premiers who could potentially challenge him, to Berlin for Sunday evening as votes are counted. He plans to demand that they either come forward with any designs to replace him — or to get in line, according to a person who spoke on condition of anonymity as deliberations take place behind closed doors.

The eight premiers sought to defuse any standoff, at least for now, with a declaration on Wednesday that they stood behind the chancellor. Restoring trust in the party will require political action, not “debates about personnel,” they wrote.
“As state premiers, we want to — and will — do our part, together with the chancellor,” the declaration read, though it stopped short of naming Merz.

Doubts remain about whether the declaration will restore the German leader’s authority. His plea to party chieftains at a meeting after the Saxony-Anhalt vote to publicly declare their support was largely met with silence, according to a participant of the closed-door meeting.

On Thursday, Merz made a pitch for the CDU’s Berlin campaign, though in the safety of the party’s national headquarters rather than a public rally. He touted signs that Europe’s biggest economy was beginning to see a turnaround.
“After 16 months, despite all criticism, some of which I share but not all — we’re on our way out of the crisis,” Merz said.

Most of the focus on Sunday will be on the result in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, another eastern state where the AfD leads in polls. The Social Democrats, who have long dominated there, are mounting a stiff challenge. But the CDU is polling in the single digits.

If Merz’s party slips under the 5% threshold to enter state parliament, it would mark the first time the CDU is ejected from a regional legislature since the federal republic was founded in 1949. To many in the party, that could be the trigger for rebellion.

For his part, Merz is banking on the lack of a succession plan among those considered likely to replace him, according to a person familiar with this thinking. The declaration was signed by Hendrik Wüst, the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, who is most often touted as a candidate — but who has his sights set on reelection in the region in April.

Bavarian premier Markus Söder, who as leader of the Christian Social Union didn’t sign the CDU document, has also harbored ambitions for Berlin. But even though the CDU and CSU campaign and caucus together on the national level, powerful figures in Merz’s party have long taken a dim view of a member of the Bavarian party in the chancellery.

Merz, who declared after the Saxony-Anhalt debacle that “giving up is not an option,” is determined to stay put, insisting that he plans to see through his agenda to overhaul Germany’s pension, healthcare and income-tax system. Despite the setbacks, Merz continues to see himself on a mission to save Germany, a person familiar with his thinking said.
But many party officials are convinced that his stewardship can only do more harm — and that, whether he remains in power after this political cycle, his departure will come sooner rather than later.

It would be a bitter path for Merz. His pledge to halve AfD support in 2018 was based on his pledge to win back voters disaffected by Angela Merkel’s centrist tack, particularly on migration. Instead, the far-right party’s surge has only strengthened, leaving a party that’s dominated German political for eight decades weakened.

items.title: PE Firms Said to Consider Fresh Bids for China Evergrande Unit
body: Private equity firms previously circling Evergrande Property Services Group Ltd. are considering making fresh offers for the Hong Kong-listed real estate management business, people familiar with the situation said.

PAG, Warburg Pincus and Trustar Capital are among firms preparing bids, the people said, asking not to be identified because the deliberations are confidential. They’re coming back into the fray after China Evergrande Group’s liquidators failed to reach an agreement with Guangdong Provincial Tourism Holdings Co., which had been in exclusive talks, according to the people.
Considerations are ongoing and might not lead to any offer, the people said.
Representatives for Evergrande’s liquidators, PAG, Trustar and Warburg Pincus declined to comment.
Evergrande Property Services said in June it was looking for potential buyers of a controlling stake after the talks with Guangdong Provincial Tourism fell apart.

The liquidation of China Evergrande, once a poster child of the country’s real estate boom, has been further complicated following last month’s life sentencing of its founder, Hui Ka Yan. He was convicted of fraud that included inflating assets and concealing liabilities. The court ordered the confiscation of Hui’s assets and his companies were fined about 15.8 billion yuan ($2.4 billion).
Evergrande’s offshore creditors are owed roughly $45 billion, and liquidators had been eyeing Hui’s estimated $7.7 billion in assets to help repay the debts.
Read More: Evergrande Creditors Owed $45 Billion Face More Complex Path

Shares of Evergrande Property Services have risen about 2% this year in Hong Kong, giving the company a market capitalization of $1.6 billion. Its first-half revenue totaled 6.9 billion yuan and net income was 517 million yuan.

items.title: Can Xi, Trump Set Up AI Guardrails Before the Tech Runs Amok?
body: Hi, this is Philip Glamann in Beijing.
Less than a week before Chinese leader Xi Jinping travels to the US to meet President Donald Trump, AI has taken center stage in the bilateral relationship.
In some ways the rivalry is straightforward. Most benchmarks show American models have a lead in performance that Washington very much wants to maintain, for military and economic reasons.
As Trump put it this week: “Whoever wins AI, wins.”

China’s models are very nearly as good, though, and their lower cost makes them appealing in developing nations that Beijing has been courting for decades. Xi used a trip to India for a BRICS summit to champion his nation’s AI vision, positioning China to lead a “community” for open-source AI.
Oddly though, there is some agreement on AI of sorts. For one thing, Trump and the Chinese government have both pushed back on fears that AI will destroy us all.

This week, Trump dismissed worries raised by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and backed by OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk as a “hoax.” Still, Trump did suggest that China could be behind those concerns, though he didn’t spell out exactly how.

China also lashed out at the fears raised by the tech titans, with one diplomat saying that “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance and serve the interests of no one.”

Both the Trump administration and officials in Beijing have their issues with Anthropic. Earlier this year, the White House was peeved because the company wanted assurances that its AI wouldn’t be used for mass surveillance of Americans or autonomous weapons deployment.

And China didn’t seem terribly pleased that Amodei singled China out in a blog post that warned about the risks of AI, as he saw them. “If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance,” he wrote.

Chinese state media later hit back, calling the slowdown idea “self-serving.” (Anthropic also accuses Chinese companies of piggybacking off its technology through “distillation” but that’s a rabbit hole for another day.)

Underscoring Beijing’s belief that it should be one of the main writers of the rules for the AI road, the English-language China Daily wrote that “a global AI-safety framework that excludes China is not quite global.”
Yet China has its own worries about AI and humanity, ones that echo those of the tech figures in the US.
On Sunday, China’s top intelligence official, Chen Yixin, wrote that use of the tech by rivals could “directly threaten China’s political security, institutional security and ideological security.”

Chen’s article, which also warned about AI’s ability to create malware to exploit weaknesses in computer systems, was significant because it was one of the clearest accounts so far on how Beijing assesses the dangers that the flourishing tech poses.

For all the heated competition on AI, both sides do in fact share similar safety concerns. That’s got some people thinking about the ways in which the two sides could cooperate. After all, the US and Soviet Union did as much on nuclear weapons.

Media entrepreneur-cum-China analyst Bill Bishop suggested in a newsletter this week that Beijing and Washington create a high-level forum that meets regularly in a third country so they can sort through their differences.
He suggested that among the first topics of discussion should be “nuclear command and control, catastrophic biological risks” and “other areas where limited but meaningful cooperation is realistic.”

It is easy to be skeptical that’ll happen, especially at the upcoming summit. After all, for all the G2 talk, areas where the two sides agree are sometimes hard to spot. And expectations for outcomes from the Xi-Trump meeting on Thursday at the White House are low.

Right now it looks like the two nations will make a limited deal on American agricultural and energy products as well as unfinished Chinese goods. In other words, just enough to extend the one-year trade truce, though maybe not for a full 12 months.
While there was some speculation China and the US would hold a meeting dedicated solely to AI issues before the summit, that never came to pass.
Right now it looks like officials in Beijing and Washington will have to have a close call with some of their worst fears on AI before they agree to hold serious talks about its dangers.
What We’re Reading, Listening to and Watching:

A major reason the Chinese government may not be particularly interested in slowing in the AI race is that the world’s second-biggest economy is increasingly reliant on the tech for growth, now and in the future.

Economic data this week was largely disappointing. One of the few bright spots was factory output beating expectations in August, mostly because AI exports have been boosted by global demand for the tech goods the nation makes.
Other than that, consumer spending and investment languished. The jobless rate saw an unexpected uptick, and home prices continued to drop.

Data also showed that loan expansion weakened far more than expected in August. That’s also worrying for the economy, though the central bank governor, Pan Gongsheng, described it as a natural development during a transition toward a new normal of slower loan growth.
The slowdown in overall financing also helps keep the debt levels stable, he wrote in an article.
Still, worries about the economy, at least other than humming factories, remain. September will be pivotal, if that’s going to change.

Without a sharp turnaround this month, the nation’s economic growth is increasingly at risk of falling below the official annual target of 4.5% to 5% for a second straight quarter after a sharp deceleration in the April-June period.

Australia & New Zealand Banking Group said GDP growth was tracking at 4.2% in July-August, less than the second-half rate needed to meet the annual target. That goal was already changed to a range to give Beijing more wiggle room.
Despite mounting pressure to ramp up stimulus so domestic demand can recover, policymakers appear to be in little hurry to do that.

Instead, they want existing measures to make good. That includes pushing state-owned banks to deploy more funding from a program that can unlock 800 billion yuan ($119 billion) for projects this year, 60% more than in 2025.
That program set up in March has been slow to get off the ground.
With a focus on major initiatives such as the Six Networks, the financing could set off a new wave of infrastructure investment in the coming months.

The Six Networks program, part of the latest five-year plan, is important because it marks the first time the nation has brought its biggest building projects under a single, integrated program, rather than developing transport, energy and communications networks separately.

The aim is to not only backstop AI ambitions, but also strengthen the manufacturing base and advance the transition to a low-carbon economy. If it succeeds, it will bolster China’s resilience to geopolitical tensions, economic shocks and natural disasters.
So it’s a big bet and a long-term one. Yet the sooner it gets rolling, the better for the economy.
Bloomberg Economics economists Chang Shu and Eric Zhu said that based on the upbeat industrial production growth, “the government is unlikely to roll out extra stimulus.”
“The path of least resistance is to accelerate input in mega projects in the pipeline to ensure growth hits the target range,” they wrote.
A weekly look at the big water cooler news in China.
Beijing’s sweeping ban on owning recreational drones in the city following a plane crash sparked debate in China this week.

While some people backed tighter security measures in the capital, others lamented the potential economic fallout. Many questioned or mocked a rule that extends to merely flying one of the devices for fun.

“Banning people from owning drones they legally purchased before the rules took effect makes little sense legally, logically or practically,” one Weibo user wrote in a post that drew more than 2,600 likes. “Isn’t that a bit ridiculous?”

The move tightened rules in place since earlier this year to cover the possession or even storage of recreational drones. The latest curbs — some of the tightest in the world — take effect in mid-November.
Drone owners have to either move their aircraft out of the city or turn to a government buyback program. The city is offering to pay up to 3,000 yuan unit.

The changes come after a small plane flew into Beijing’s Citic Tower in June, killing the pilot and injuring 13 others. The incident took place just miles from the headquarters of the ruling Communist Party and residence of top leaders.
Officials said the pilot deliberately crashed. The aircraft also nearly collided with a commercial jet before impact.
Some people said they supported the policy, arguing that the curbs reflect security needs in the capital, even though that would mean an end to things like aerial photography.

Others pointed to possible economic implications. “The low-altitude economy can bid farewell to Beijing,” one person wrote, referring to a sector that policymakers have promoted as a new growth driver.
Many reacted with humor. One Internet user highlighted posts from drone owners jokingly trying to dispose of their aircraft.
“Who wants one? Free, just pay the shipping. Help fulfill the dream of someone who’s never owned a DJI,” read one post, referring to a leading Chinese maker of the drones.

items.title: EU Migration, Russian Attacks Prompt European Border Wall Building Flurry
body: Heavy with water, Wafae Atid’s shirt clings to her body. Her hair is slicked back, her face is damp, but she looks elated. Just meters away, the fence separating Africa from Europe towers into the dark sky. Atid did not climb over it. She swam around.

In a now-deleted video posted to Instagram on July 31, the 28-year-old Moroccan stands on wet rocks as a crowd of young men scramble out of the murky water behind her into Spain. Atid, who later told Spanish journalists she is neither rich nor poor, was among the 70,000 people who rushed the border between Morocco and Ceuta at the end of July. Critics have described her as a harraga — irregular migration — influencer, whose success encourages others to attempt to reach Europe even though it may no longer be possible to copy her route.

The day after Atid’s crossing, Spanish authorities responded to the rush on Ceuta’s border by installing a 500-meter (1,640-foot) floating barrier along the water. Last week, the European Commission announced more than €100 million ($115 million) in funding to strengthen that border, including for thermal cameras, buoy systems and underwater drones. These are only the latest additions to a barrier Spain first erected in 1993, justified at the time as the price of joining the European Union’s borderless Schengen Zone. Over the past three decades, what began as a simple wire fence has been repeatedly heightened, reinforced and outfitted with new technology.

Spain built the Ceuta fence just four years after another European wall came down. Images of Berliners tearing down a symbol of a divided continent were broadcast around the world, and the fall of the Berlin wall came to symbolize a continent embracing globalization. But even as Europe was dismantling barriers within, new ones were appearing at its edges. In retrospect, Ceuta, not Berlin, may have been the better omen of what was to come.
Read More: Europe Never Recovered From the Fall of the Berlin Wall

When it was built, the Ceuta fence was an anomaly — Schengen’s first. But by 2022, more than 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) of fencing encircled the EU. Today, walls trace the external borders of Estonia, Finland, Hungary, Latvia and Poland. Historian Timothy Garton Ash has called this “Europe’s reverse 1989.”

Their purpose has expanded too. Barriers erected during the migration crisis of the 2010s were intended to stop migrants from Syria or Afghanistan arriving through Turkey or Greece. In the 2020s, construction shifted east, as countries bordering Russia and Belarus sought protection first from “weaponized” migration and then from the threat of war spilling across their borders. More recently, a series of drone incursions into European territory spurred plans for a drone wall. Climate change has added fears of future mass migration, and last year a Finnish Border Guard official said the country’s new eastern barrier had been built to withstand threats Finland didn’t even know about yet.

For an anxious Europe, walls offer the promise of control in an increasingly uncertain world. Olga Cielemecka, a researcher at the University of Eastern Finland, calls their proliferation “a new era of enclosures.” Walls, she argues, provide a tangible, quick-fix answer to problems that are often complex and amorphous.

The July rush into Ceuta, for example, was blamed on a tangle of inequality, smugglers, social media and the actions — or inaction — of Moroccan authorities. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez answered with something far simpler: a big orange barrier floating in the Gibraltar Strait. Legally, the sea barrier can be seen as a response to a Spanish Supreme Court ruling that said only migrants who crossed a physical barrier could be fast-tracked and returned to Morocco. But it was also a visible reaction to public demand for action. In a September survey, 82% of Spaniards supported increasing fencing at the borders.
Read More: The Ceuta Migrant Crossing Didn’t Need a Mastermind

The European Commission has tried for years to steer member states toward invisible, high-tech walls, while refusing to finance fences or barbed wire. A Commission spokesperson declined to say whether that position had changed. Even so, member states continue to pay for their own concrete, razor wire and metal.

The imagery is part of the point, Cielemecka says: Technology cannot replicate the psychological effect of a physical fence. “They are such a powerful message that communicates to potential crossers, ‘You are not welcome,’” she says, “and to domestic audiences, ‘You are being protected.’”

Nor is the impulse to build walls confined to Europe. In his 2016 election bid, Donald Trump famously campaigned on “Build That Wall.” Algeria has invested in sand walls, fences and barbed wire to secure its borders against smugglers, migrants and armed groups. The use of walls is now unprecedented in modern history, says Élisabeth Vallet, a border scholar at the University of Québec in Montréal and a professor at the Royal Military College Saint-Jean in Canada. When World War II ended, there were fewer than five such walls worldwide. By the end of the Cold War, there were 12. Today there are more than 100, according to Vallet’s tally. “The wall has become the panacea,” she says.

Yet a wall rarely eliminates pressure on a border; it changes the way that pressure is expressed. Determined crossers can move toward less-protected stretches, take more dangerous routes or develop new ways through. After Lithuania lined most of its border with Belarus with concrete and barbed wire in 2022, authorities recently discovered underground tunnels. “What we are trying to do with the wall is like trying to retain water with our hands,” says Vallet. “It will work for a second or two, but then the water will overflow.”

Throughout its three-decade history, Ceuta’s border fence has failed to deter attempts to cross into Spain. In 1999, what the Spanish press called a 2.5-meter “flimsy wire” barrier was upgraded to “armored metal.” In 2005 hundreds of people were still able to climb over it, though one person bled to death after becoming entangled in razor wire.

Successive governments have reshaped Spain’s border barriers according to their politics, says Rut Bermejo Casado, a nonresident senior fellow at the Elcano Royal Institute, a Spanish think tank. A socialist government removed some razor wire in 2007; a right-wing government restored it in 2013. Thousands more people climbed the fence in 2017, by which point it stood 6 meters tall. By 2022 the Sánchez administration had removed Ceuta’s razor wire once again. Since 2019, Spain has spent €37 million modernizing the border with night-vision cameras and sensors, an amount that does not include the latest upgrades. Today, it is not a single fence but three.

Border states can become trapped in similar cycles of fortification. Poland’s barrier along its frontier with Belarus, built in 2022, was supplemented with an electronic fence the following year. By 2025, the Polish Border Guard decided it needed a second physical fence to stop people who managed to  climb over the first. Israel’s high-tech Gaza barrier, which included an underground wall studded with sensors, suffered a catastrophic breach on Oct. 7, 2023. Recent satellite imagery shows the Israeli military is now building another large sand barrier inside Gaza, parallel to the existing fence.

Upgraded fences aren’t just higher — or wider, as in the case of Ceuta — but also thicker, absorbing more land. Border barriers are often flanked by buffer zones closed to the public. In Finland, where the “border zone” can extend up to 4 kilometers, fishermen and academics must apply for permits that can be denied. Radar systems, motion and vibration sensors, and CCTV extend that reach further still.

Europe has also exported much of this technology to countries along migration routes. Libyan and Tunisian coast guards, for example, have been equipped with sonar and radar to police the Mediterranean, says Ahlam Chemlali, migration researcher and co-director of the Center for Coercion and Accountability at Denmark’s Aalborg University. Migrants now encounter Europe’s borders as far away as the Sahara, she says. “European borders have moved deep inside the African continent.”

If the goal is simply to reduce irregular crossings, the approach seems to be working: Such crossings into the EU have fallen to their lowest levels since 2021. (Ceuta’s own figures, however, show fluctuation rather than a steady decline.) But there have also been violent consequences. At least 100 people died trying to cross into Ceuta in July, while another 100 have died at the Polish-Belarus border since 2021, according to a September report.

And fortifying Europe’s borders does little to address the reasons people move in the first place, from conflict and inequality to the promise of a different life glimpsed through social media. By concentrating would-be migrants on the far side of hardened borders, often with few legal routes available, Europe can also leave them more vulnerable to governments willing to use migration as political leverage. “If you have regular pathways, then people will likely be less exploitable by hostile parties that take advantage of them,” says Davide Colombi, a migration researcher at think tank CEPS in Brussels.

What has endured through the long history of humans building walls is a tendency to confuse what they can accomplish, says Raphael Cohen, a senior political analyst at Rand. Walls can buy governments time by reducing violence and migration, he argues, but only temporarily. “Building a wall is often the easy button,” says Cohen.

Yet the allure of the wall is unlikely to disappear; as architecture, they capture a mood of deep uncertainty. “We live in this moment of extensive crisis,” says Jenny Stümer, research coordinator at Heidelberg University’s Käte Hamburger Center for Apocalyptic and Post-Apocalyptic Studies. “We have the climate crisis, we have political crises, economic crisis, and they all converge at this moment.”
Walls offer the promise of continuity, Stümer says: a way to protect the status quo. “We erect some walls to make sure that no one comes in and takes anything away from us.”

items.title: GCash Owner Gets Approval for Up to $1.5 Billion Philippines IPO
body: The company behind GCash, the biggest mobile wallet app in the Philippines, received approval from the country’s stock exchange operator of an initial public offering of as much as 92.3 billion pesos ($1.47 billion), clearing the final regulatory hurdle for a record debut.

Mynt Inc. has received the Philippine Stock Exchange’s notice of approval for its listing application, shareholder Globe Telecom Inc. said in a disclosure, adding that it will disclose further details at the appropriate time.

Mynt will offer as many as 1.61 billion primary shares and as many as 6.42 billion secondary shares for as much as 10 pesos each, giving it a market capitalization of 668.9 billion pesos at the high end, the stock exchange said in a notice, with net proceeds earmarked to expand digital financial services, product development, and general corporate purposes. The final price will be set on Oct. 1, with allocations from Oct. 6 to 12 and a listing on Oct. 20.

The IPO will be the first listing this year in the Philippines, where the stock market has grappled with low trading volumes, a spate of delistings and a lack of investor confidence. Listings last year has raised about $530 million, the most since a record year in 2021, largely thanks to the debut of Maynilad Water Services Inc. in October.

Mynt’s key shareholders include Globe, Ant International and Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group Inc. GCash began as Globe’s text-based money transfer service in 2004 and has grown to 90 million registered users. The app has expanded into credit, investments and savings services from payments, becoming ubiquitous since the pandemic.
Read More: GCash Owner Gauges Demand for $1.5 Billion Philippines IPO

Market participants have been waiting for the IPO for some time. Regulators have eased the rules on the minimum public float requirement to encourage large listings. The deal could exceed the 2021 IPO of Monde Nissin Corp., which raised about 55.9 billion pesos. The company offers investors exposure to a population of more than 110 million people who are increasingly using digital payments rather than cash.

Morgan Stanley & Co. International PLC, J.P. Morgan Securities Plc and UBS AG Singapore Branch are joint global coordinators and joint bookrunners, while Jefferies Singapore Limited, CLSA Limited and The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited, Singapore Branch are the international joint bookrunners. BPI Capital Corp., BDO Capital & Investment Corp., AB Capital & Investment Corp. and First Metro Investment Corp. are the domestic lead underwriters.

items.title: Bond Investors See Region of Opportunity in Eastern Europe
body: Hi, this is Andrea in Prague. Welcome to our weekly newsletter on what’s shaping economics and investments from the Baltic Sea to the Balkans. You can subscribe here.

It hasn’t been a great time of late to be a fixed-income investor. Government bonds have been slumping, weighed down by stubbornly high inflation, a flood of new corporate offerings that are competing for money and concerns over budget deficits. Fund managers are increasingly looking east as they hunt the best opportunities in Europe’s choppy markets.

Bulgaria, Hungary and Lithuania are among their top picks given an improved economic and fiscal backdrop, as well as the yields on offer, a combination that’s harder to find among their western neighbors. Political changes and the stringent requirements to be in the euro region, further boost the investment case, as my colleagues Alice Gledhill and George Nixon reported.

Dickie Hodges, manager of the $2.5 billion Nomura Global Dynamic Bond Fund, says 15% of his holdings are bonds from Eastern Europe, the highest in his career. He’s particularly keen on new euro member Bulgaria.

James Ringer at Schroders, meanwhile, said Hungary is his top pick out of all sovereign markets globally. The amount of Hungarian bonds and bills held by foreign investors reached a record high in July, according to data from the debt agency compiled by Bloomberg.

At MFS Investment Management, Annalisa Piazza holds Lithuanian debt to help anchor her portfolio during bouts of volatility. Latvia and Lithuania are the best-performing euro-denominated bonds this year, based on a Bloomberg index tracking sovereign debt.

Romania is also getting popular, albeit for different reasons. Mired by surging debt and political paralysis, the country is years off the euro adoption it seeks. Some investors are treating Romanian bonds as the European Union’s only junk-rated sovereign debt, with high yields proving attractive despite turmoil in Bucharest, as Peter Laca and Andra Timu reported this week.
Latvia: Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs signaled he wants Lufthansa to retain its stake in Air Baltic as the government looks to turn around the nation’s bankrupt flag carrier.

Ukraine: New Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said his nation faces sweeping cuts to its war-ravaged budget unless lawmakers adopt unpopular measures needed to access billions in western aid ahead of winter.

Czech Republic: The government is mulling privatizing parts of explosives maker Explosia and Prague airport operator Letiste Praha and will decide by early next year whether to proceed, Deputy Prime Minister Karel Havlicek said in an interview.

Croatia: Koncar-Elektroindustrija, the biggest net exporter in the country, expects to invest more than €800 million ($923 million) in Europe, the US, and the Middle East in the coming years, top executive Gordan Kolak told Bloomberg.

Hungary: Prime Minister Peter Magyar’s mission to move on from Viktor Orban continued. He shut down his predecessor’s controversial communist terror museum, a real estate tycoon was detained in an embezzlement probe and details emerged about abuse and malnourishment in the childcare system.

Poland’s first generation of post-communist entrepreneurs is increasingly hunting for new investments at home and abroad. That’s creating opportunities for the financial services industry to manage larger pools of money, as my colleague Konrad Krasuski in Warsaw reported this week. The number of Polish residents with assets exceeding $30 million has more than doubled to about 3,000 since 2021, the fastest increase among countries tracked by property consultancy Knight Frank.

Hundreds of people protested in Kosovo after judges in The Hague sentenced former President Hashim Thaci to 25 years in prison for war crimes. Many were clad in flags that were a symbol of the Kosovo Liberation Army that Thaci led through the 1998-99 war with Serbia. His conviction, which he can appeal, challenges one of the main narratives on which Kosovo’s statehood was built: that the KLA took up arms to protect its people and liberate the country. Prime Minister Albin Kurti said the verdict was an “unacceptable injustice.”

items.title: Iron Ore Set for Weekly Gain Despite Weak China Steel Demand
body: Iron ore was headed for a weekly gain after recovering from a sharp decline earlier in the week, even as weak steel demand and shrinking mill margins weighed on the outlook.

Singapore futures have gained about 1% this week, rising for a third day to as high as $97.45 a ton on Friday. The rebound erased losses that pushed prices of the steelmaking ingredient to the lowest close since mid-August on Tuesday.

Chinese steel demand typically strengthens ahead of the Golden Week holiday in October, boosting production, but inventory drawdowns have been modest and prices remain at the weaker end of their seasonal range.

China’s Iron and Steel Association this week urged mills to strictly enforce production controls and reduce inventories. The call was backed by 44 major steelmakers including China Baowu Steel Group Corp. and points to persistent oversupply.

“The fact that CISA is calling for a market rebalancing now confirms that a local steel surplus is a function of other bear factors, not just a seasonal pullback in activity,” Tom Price, an analyst at Panmure Liberum, said in a note released Thursday.
Read More: Brazil’s Smaller Iron Ore Miners Battered by Shipping Costs

Steel mill profitability remained below 10%, according to Mysteel, even as pig iron output and capacity utilization edged higher. Integrated mills have increased purchases of imported iron ore ahead of the holidays, but near-term demand has improved only marginally, the data provider said.

“Weak domestic steel demand lies at the heart of the poor profitability of China’s steel sector this year,” said Vivek Dhar, an analyst at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. “But loss‑making steel production in China will likely compel China Mineral Resources Group, which represents Chinese steelmakers, to push harder to structurally lower iron ore prices with iron ore miners.”
Iron ore futures rose 1.1% to $97.45 a ton at 12:25 p.m. local time, while yuan-priced futures on the Dalian exchange also advanced. Shanghai steel futures declined.

items.title: Korea's Lee Says $350 Billion US Deal Causing 'Sleepless Nights'
body: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said talks with the US over projects tied to Seoul’s $350 billion investment commitment were causing him to lose sleep, with discussions reopening after he found parts of a nearly completed deal hard to accept.
“I myself have spent sleepless nights thinking about this,” Lee said at a press conference Friday. “It carries enormous weight.”

The comments highlight the challenges Seoul faces in implementing the investment package agreed with the Trump administration last year, as the two sides work toward selecting the first projects under the deal. The delay has angered the US administration, with President Donald Trump abruptly scaling back joint military drills last month.

Lee said South Korea would only pursue projects deemed commercially viable, a condition Seoul insisted on including in its agreement with Washington after “very difficult” negotiations. The issue has become more important as the two countries move from the broader agreement to discussions over specific investments, he said.
South Korea’s investment pledge mirrors a similar commitment by neighboring Japan to avert higher US tariffs, though Tokyo has moved more quickly to put its $550 billion plan into action.
The talks have resumed between Seoul and Washington with the aim of structuring projects that don’t undermine Seoul’s national interests and provide benefits to both countries, Lee said.
“We should not be swayed by any relationship, pressure or coercion, though I’m not saying the US is doing that,” Lee said. “I’m simply stating the principle I believe in.”

Earlier this year, Washington complained about what it sees as a lack of follow-through on Seoul’s investment commitments. While the two nations had been nearing an announcement on the first project, South Korea recently asked for more time to fine-tune the deal.
Lee told reporters that South Korea would not deploy troops or military assets to take part in or intervene in the war, reiterating that its principle of non-involvement would remain unchanged.

items.title: Indonesia's New Finance Chief to Keep $17 Billion in State Banks
body: Indonesia’s new finance minister will retain the policy of his predecessor of keeping about $17 billion in the government’s standby funds with state lenders to help boost borrowing and economic activity.
The so-called SAL funds, estimated at about 299 trillion rupiah to date, will be placed through July 2027, Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara said at a budget briefing in Jakarta on Friday.

“SAL placements are being carried out and managed in such a way so as not to disrupt banking stability or the economy,” Suahasil said, adding that his ministry will communicate monthly with the banking sector and the central bank — where the funds were previously placed.

“Later, when the withdrawal takes place, the Ministry of Finance will coordinate to ensure there is no gap in funding availability within the banking sector,” said Astera Primanto Bhakti, director-general of Treasury.
Shares of state-owned PT Bank Mandiri, PT Bank Negara Indonesia, PT Bank Rakyat Indonesia and PT Bank Tabungan Negara held earlier losses on Friday.

One of the most prominent, and at times most controversial, measures introduced by former Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa had been to flush the banking system with cash in a bid to boost economic growth.

Purbaya, who was removed from his post earlier this week, had broke from the ministry’s conventional practice of keeping the funds with the central bank, which oversaw the liquidity management in the financial system as part of its monetary policy.

items.title: Najib Wins House Arrest in Malaysia's 1MDB Corruption Case
body: Malaysia’s jailed former Prime Minister Najib Razak, a central figure in the country’s biggest corruption scandal, has been granted a conditional pardon that allows him to serve the remainder of his jail term under house arrest, offering a reprieve for the ex-premier after spending the last four years in prison.

Najib’s house arrest granted by King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar however is conditional upon Najib paying a 50 million ringgit ($12.3 million) fine as part of his 1MDB sentence, the Prime Minister’s Department said in a statement on Friday. The house arrest runs through August 2028.

The decision comes after the nation’s Pardons Board, chaired by the king, met for the second time in as many weeks to consider Najib’s bid for a royal pardon. The king deferred a decision on his application, while granting clemency to other prisoners during its Sept. 11 meeting.
The government didn’t disclose the conditions of Najib’s house arrest in its statement, including whether his movements, visitors or communications will be restricted.

The outcome appears to offer a middle ground between the competing positions of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s coalition partners amid an increasingly uneasy alliance ahead of the next general election. House arrest falls short of the freedom sought by Najib’s former party — whose support remains crucial to the ruling coalition — while allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence outside prison.
Allowing Najib to leave prison would risk alienating supporters of Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan who see his conviction as a test of the government’s commitment to fighting corruption.
Najib, 73, was sentenced in 2020 to 12 years in prison and fined 210 million ringgit ($52 million) over his role in the multibillion dollar 1MDB scandal. He began serving his sentence in August 2022.

Najib’s downfall came after he was accused of siphoning off billions of dollars raised by the country’s sovereign wealth, with the help of bankers from prestige firms including Goldman Sachs Group Inc.

The taint of corruption also led to his party, the United Malays National Organisation, losing power in 2018 for the first time since the country’s independence. The country’s oldest party has been part of Anwar’s coalition since 2022.

Najib remains popular within UMNO, which has repeatedly pushed for his release or a royal pardon, creating an awkward tension within the ruling coalition. Pakatan Harapan has said those convicted in high-profile corruption and abuse-of-power cases should serve their full court-imposed sentences.

UMNO has also performed well in recent state polls at the expense of Pakatan, leading to it calling for early elections, while Anwar’s relationship with current UMNO chief Zahid Hamidi, who is deputy prime minister, is said to have deteriorated.
Read More: Anwar’s Bond With Malaysia Deputy PM Said to Vastly Deteriorate
Zahid expressed his party’s gratitude to the king in a Facebook post on Friday, and said UMNO will launch a fund to help ease Najib’s burden in paying the 50 million ringgit fine.

Friday’s decision is Najib’s second royal reprieve, after his sentence was reduced before in 2024. Under then King Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah, the Pardons Board halved his sentence to six years and cut his fine to 50 million ringgit. Under that decision, Najib was due to be released in August 2028, although an additional year could be added if he failed to pay the fine.

The former premier was also convicted for another 1MDB-related corruption case last December and sentenced to another 15 years in prison and a 11.4 billion ringgit fine. Najib is appealing that ruling at the Court of Appeal. The royal reprieve doesn’t cover his second conviction.

While the reprieve keeps him out of prison, Najib won’t be able to return to active politics at least until the end of his current house arrest period. He also needs to overturn the second 1MDB conviction.

The Federal Territories Pardons Board is chaired by the king and includes Attorney-General of Malaysia Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar, Hannah Yeoh, a cabinet minister, and three other members appointed by the king.
