items.title: Forget Oktoberfest: Munich's Top Restaurants for Italian Food, Ramen, Value
body: Welcome to Five Top Tables, a column from Bloomberg Pursuits to guide your dining decisions in major cities around the world, including New York, London, Singapore, Mexico City, Mumbai and Tokyo.

If you’re one of the 6 million-plus people heading to Oktoberfest, prepare to spend money. The famed festival, which runs from Sept. 19 to Oct. 4, is making headlines for record prices, with liters of beer set to cost as much as €15.90 ($18.20) in the more popular tents.

And come hungry. There’s an emphasis this year on locally sourced and organic foods, a major boost for Bavaria’s sustainable farming movement. Look for the snacks that pair well with the trademark lagers, including white sausages (Weißwürste), pork knuckles (Schweinshaxen), huge, delectable pretzels (Brez’n), and other local favorites. They’re all over the festival grounds, but we recommend going to higher-end locations, such as the tent of the celebrated deli Käfer Wiesn-Schänke.

Now more than ever, though, Munich’s food scene has more going on than traditional fare for the lederhosen and dirndl set. While the city loves its Bavarian heritage, it’s also home to 1.6 million people, about half of whom have international roots. That’s one reason for the wealth of great Turkish, Greek and Indian restaurants. Locals refer to Munich as the “northernmost Italian city,” a nod to the relatively sunny climate (by German standards anyway), proximity to southern Europe and the presence of at least one notably good Italian restaurant in almost every neighborhood.

Whether you’re visiting for the beer fest or business (or both), we’ve rounded up places that capture the city’s cosmopolitan energy, modern sensibilities and abiding love for tradition. And speaking of Mediterranean character, we’re including an Italian grill in the heart of Munich’s shopping and culture hub that’s popular on the Bloomberg Terminal’s DINE <GO>, where the food community rates their favorite places.

Seafood is never the first thing you associate with Munich, the land of pork and beef. But the newly opened Das Fogosch is here to change your mind. The intimate, modern bistro is located in the hip, restaurant- and bar-stocked neighborhood of Maxvorstadt, a short U-Bahn ride or 15-minute stroll from the city center. It’s the fourth Munich restaurant from Austrian chef Jürgen Wolfsgruber, whose flagship location, Sparkling Bistro, has a Michelin star.

Here the chef forgoes the fancy trimmings. The small menu and daily specials depend on the quality of fish his suppliers have available. The €35 prix fixe lunch might start with a plate of cured river trout and crisp potato rösti with salad and sliced radishes. A standout tagliatelle bathed in green pesto is paired with seared octopus tentacles and finished with a light seafood foam. A special of pan-seared Arctic char (€28 per 100 grams, or 3.5 ounces) also benefits from juicy braised tomatoes and wilted spinach.

A crisp, alcohol-free Jörg Geiger sparkling cuvée made from apples and pears with an infusion of hay flowers makes for a good all-purpose pairing, and there’s a strong selection of bottles, especially whites, rosés and sparkling wines. Amalienstrasse 81; dasfogosch.com

It’s impossible to miss Pfistermühle in the heart of Munich’s Old Town: Look for the vine-covered building that seems to jump straight off the pages of a Grimm fairytale. (It’s also convenient, just a two-minute walk from the world-famous Hofbräuhaus.)

The upscale Bavarian restaurant, which doubles as an escape from Oktoberfest craziness, has deep roots. Pfistermühle is an old-fashioned name for “bakery mill,” highlighting the site’s centuries-long role in supplying bread to Munich’s royal court. But like so much of the city, the building was heavily damaged during World War II and later restored to preserve its 16th century character. In recent years its management has modernized the interior and menu.

In accordance with its name, Pfistermühle offers a rich, hearty bread service with seasonal butter as an appetizer. You might not want to eat anything else. But carry on. The Rinderfilet, aka beef tenderloin (€38), is wonderfully juicy and flavorful on its own, then further upgraded with a golden-brown bone-marrow crust and thick shallot sauce. There are also a few vegetable dishes on the menu, including a €14 creamy, seasonal soup of chanterelle mushrooms, as well as linguine studded with porcinis and accented with Alpine cheese for €29.

Because of Pfistermühle’s striking ivy-covered facade, the pedestrianized street out front is a hot spot for tourists looking for a quick selfie. But inside it’s cozy and intimate, and the space includes several quiet nooks and private rooms that can be reserved for serious conversations, making it especially popular with the business crowd. The restaurant is connected to the four-star Platzl Hotel — particularly convenient for work trips. Pfisterstraße 4; pfistermuehle.de

Munich has a well-earned reputation in Germany for being expensive. It has the country’s highest rents and enough pricey restaurants to give budget-minded consumers pause. But the city also has plenty of good-value eateries, including Takumi. The ramen shop sits on Buttermelcherstrasse, a few minutes’ stroll from one of Munich’s prettier squares, Gärtnerplatz. That puts it in the heart of the Glockenbachviertel, a hip neighborhood unafraid to break with Bavarian traditions — as illustrated by one beloved local pub that’s banned visitors from wearing lederhosen and dirndls.
This popular ramen chain started out in Düsseldorf and has expanded to more than 80 locations across Europe. But its chicken- and vegan-oriented concept was first developed in Munich.

Crucial ingredients are sourced from Sapporo, the northern Japanese city famed for its ramen culture. The attraction here is less bargain-basement pricing than how much food you get for the money. A shoyu ramen costs €14.50, miso €16.50 and yuzu-shio €15.50. The unusually extensive plant-based selection includes vegan options of all of the above for a few euros less. The portions are large enough that a bowl easily works as a full meal. You choose whether you want the spicy, richer ramens or a lighter yuzu-shio with citrus notes.

The space is small and casual, with closely packed tables and counter seating. Its popularity can mean a wait at peak hours, especially for groups. If you visit during lunchtime on weekdays, you can add an extra side and cold tea for €3.90. Beer and other beverages are also available, but the main appeal is a filling lunch in one of Munich’s hottest neighborhoods for less than €20. Buttermelcherstraße 17; takumimunich.com/gaertnerplatz

This is the kind of bistro you look for in Paris, but with friendlier service. At Petit Fritz, set on a busy street in the trendy Schwabing neighborhood, you can sit at the little tables out front or inside amid the distinctly Parisian decor, with chrome lamps, leather tables and slouchy sofas. There’s a choice of the darker, moodier main area or the brighter Wintergarten out back.

The restaurant, which doesn’t take reservations, specializes in tartines, a term that sounds more sophisticated than the “open sandwich” English translation. In practice they’re little works of art, with fancy toppings including warm smoked halibut (market price) accented with drops of sour cream and horseradish on lightly fried sourdough bread. More adventurous diners can order the tête de veau (€13) or a classic, oozy Camembert au gratin (€17.50). The oyster selection is fantastic; the grander fruits de mer platter (€26.50) adds shrimp and clams to the mix. At night the menu extends to steak frites (€38.50) with a 220-gram entrecôte and sauce béarnaise, as well as a moules-frites (€24.50) alternative.

The wine list is strong on by-the-glass offerings that run the length and breadth of France. A glass of Canard-Duchêne cuvée Léonie brut goes for €15.50. And, like its sister location Chez Fritz in Munich’s Haidhausen neighborhood, the restaurant works for either a quick planned lunch or a languorous dinner that lasts late into the evening. Hohenzollernstraße 9; instagram.com/petit_fritz

For the ultimate power meal in Munich, Brenner Grill is practically unbeatable. This capacious, upscale eatery is located in the heart of the city’s high-end cultural scene, near the start of Maximilianstrasse, Munich’s luxury shopping destination, and right behind the Bavarian State Opera. The place opened in 2003, but it feels decades older. That’s partly because it occupies a nearly 11,000-square-foot hall that once served as royal stables at the urban palace of Bavaria’s long-ruling Wittelsbach family.

There are plenty of seating options in the space, which holds about 400 guests, including in the chic lounge up front as well as the pasta and grill dining areas, separated by decorative wrought-iron partitions and massive stone columns. The grill section, which boasts an open fireplace, has an especially warm ambiance for chilly nights. On warm days, head for the large outdoor terrace.

True to its equestrian roots, Brenner is a workhorse. Except for Sunday, when working hours are shorter, it opens at 8:30 a.m. every day and doesn’t close before midnight. At breakfast you’ll see updated Bavarian staples such as a pretzel with butter (€3.20) and lighter options like Bircher muesli (€8).

But in general the cuisine blends northern Italian and Bavarian favorites — from Milan to Munich, the owners say. The reasonably priced €17.50 lunch special includes a colorful fennel and carrot salad, fresh-baked bread and a meat, fish or vegetarian main course. Recently that included a tender char fillet and a delightfully crispy artichoke frittata. On the regular menu, Sardinian fregola (€23) is a mix of toasted pearls of pasta with red-wine-braised beef cheek, pan-fried porcinis and a bright herb salsa. Then there’s the hefty, 220-gram fillet of 21-day dry-aged beef (€52.50). Along with an extensive wine and cocktail list, the booze-free homemade lemonade (€7.50) is refreshing without being overly sweet.
“This is Munich’s answer to so many Milanese restaurants — a blend of carefree cafe, restaurant and general schmooze fest” is a DINE <GO> user’s assessment. Maximilianstraße 15; brennergrill.de/en

items.title: SocGen's Krupa to Unveil New Targets With 'Easy Wins' Behind Him
body: Slawomir Krupa is set to unveil his new plan for Societe Generale SA on Monday, hoping to avoid a repeat of his first capital markets day as CEO when shares of the French lender slumped 12%.
Three years on, his turnaround has gathered pace, though analysts remain cautious.

Krupa has created “a credible long-term delivery story,” but the “easy wins are largely behind us,” JPMorgan Chase & Co. analyst Delphine Lee wrote in a note earlier this month, when she downgraded shares of the French lender. SocGen, she argued, has limited scope for earnings and distribution surprises.

Krupa, a former investment banker, is looking to win back market share without jeopardizing the capital strength that he only just restored. After cutting costs and selling units to put the lender on a more solid footing, his efforts to pivot toward growth have shown mixed results, with SocGen’s traders struggling to keep up with Wall Street in recent quarters and political turmoil clouding the prospects at home in France.
That leaves Krupa, 52, with few options for bold announcements when he unveils the next step in his strategy on Sept. 21.

Investors, analysts and people inside the company expect more ambitious profitability goals, supported by a new round of costs cuts, mainly at the French retail bank. The CEO, who’s already announced almost 3,000 job reductions since taking over, will likely also outline targeted investments in growth, though with an eye toward limiting their capital consumption, people familiar with his thinking said, asking for anonymity to discuss private information.

“While growth may feature more prominently than at the previous capital markets day, we still expect a focus on costs to be a key lever to lift up profitability,” Morgan Stanley analyst Giulia Aurora Miotto wrote in a note. She expects SocGen to target a return on tangible equity above 13% and a cost-to-income ratio of below 53% by 2029.
A spokesperson for the French lender declined to comment.

Krupa took over as CEO at a time when SocGen had only started to recover from losses in the pandemic and a costly exit from Russia. Known for a direct style of communicating, he initially struggled to persuade investors and employees when he unveiled a strategy at the start of his tenure that was focused on strengthening capital, selling units and setting more realistic targets.

The CEO shook up the top management ranks, replacing the head of the French retail business and the chief financial officer, among others. He also ended a generous work-from-home policy, cut managerial roles and brought in external consultants to identify ways to improve efficiency, according to people familiar with the matter.

The disruption eventually paid off, with the shares more than tripling over the past two years. SocGen is now trading at almost 0.8 times its book value, still one of the lowest among European banks, but well ahead of the 0.3 times when Krupa took the reins.

The shares hit the highest price in more than 18 years this summer, taking them to levels last seen before the historic trading scandal linked to rogue trader Jerome Kerviel in 2008. Krupa himself appears to be more approachable and confident now at conferences, say analysts and investors, pointing to conversations they had with the CEO.
“The progress made over the past three years means Societe Generale is no longer a takeover target,” said Nicolas Darbo, a partner at consultancy Accuracy who focuses on the finance sector.

That doesn’t mean SocGen can play an active role itself in the wave of consolidation that’s currently reshaping European finance. Cross-town rival BNP Paribas SA catapulted its asset management business into Europe’s top ranks with the acquisition of Axa IM last year, while Credit Agricole SA has moved to strengthen its position in Italy. Italy’s UniCredit SpA is nearing control of Germany’s Commerzbank AG.

Such deals aren’t an option for Krupa, who is focusing instead on cost cuts and targeted investments to strengthen the investment bank. The latter has struggled in recent quarters to keep up with peers in securities trading, particularly in fixed income. John Estrada, the former global head of foreign exchange, and Francisco Oliveira, who co-headed the global markets business, left the firm this year.

In a bid to bolster the trading unit, SocGen has recently started offering cash prime brokerage for the first time, Bloomberg News has reported. In the US, it hired to strengthen the business of advising on stock and bond sales, and is looking to add tech-focused bankers after last year opening an office in Menlo Park. The bank is also interested in financing data centers in the country, according to people familiar with the matter.

The CEO previously led the US unit from the New York office for five years, and SocGen was among the firms working on the record SpaceX public offering this year. While the mandate was a win, people inside the bank said they were disappointed by the fees it earned in the junior role as joint book-running manager for retail shares being offered in Europe.

At home in France, Krupa last year tapped Alexis Kohler, a former top adviser to President Emmanuel Macron, to strengthen the SocGen’s relationships with the establishment and boost its advisory business.

“One of the key focus areas for investment banking today is to strengthen our advisory and primary equity activities,” Krupa said in late July. “Investment banking also needs to strengthen its strategic dialogue with corporate clients.”

Krupa has also highlighted the need to boost profitability, telling the annual shareholder meeting in May that SocGen was still “at the bottom of the class in terms of efficiency.” The bank’s cost-income ratio was just below 60% in the second quarter, in line with its target for this year but near the bottom of its peer group. That’s also true for the return on equity.

To raise such metrics, analysts and investors expect SocGen to announce a new round of cost cuts, focused mainly on the retail bank and the vehicle leasing subsidiary Ayvens. Any associated headcount reduction is expected to rely on natural attrition rather than forced redundancies, according to the people.

SocGen is also expected to join peers in highlighting the use of artificial intelligence to further improve profitability. The digital bank, known as Boursobank, will likely be a source of growth in the new plan and contribute more significantly to profit, Krupa has said.

One thing that remains largely outside the CEO’s control, however, is the political and fiscal turmoil in France, which is facing a presidential election next year. SocGen is somewhat more exposed to the French economy because its domestic retail business accounts for about a third of revenue, compared with around 15% at BNP and Credit Agricole, according to Sharath Kumar, an analyst at Deutsche Bank Research.

“The turnaround phase focused on rebuilding capital, restoring profitability and simplifying the group is largely complete,” Kumar says. “The key investor question is whether management can set sufficiently ambitious targets while remaining grounded in a challenging French macroeconomic and political backdrop.”

items.title: ECB to Hold Fire Until Final Rate Hike in December, Survey Shows
body: The European Central Bank will wait until December before delivering a final interest-rate increase to quell inflation triggered by conflict in the Middle East, according to economists.

Respondents in a Bloomberg survey expect the Governing Council to lift the deposit rate to 2.75% at its last meeting of the year, skipping the next opportunity to do so in late October. In the last round, analysts predicted that September’s quarter-point increase would be the end-point of this cycle.

Expectations have shifted in recent weeks as oil and natural gas prices jumped. The ECB also boosted its inflation forecast last week, supporting predictions that more tightening will be necessary to deliver the 2% goal. Investors are betting on at least three more hikes.

Officials also foresee further tightening, people familiar with the matter have said, though they haven’t taken a clear view on when it should happen. Irish policymaker Gabriel Makhlouf told Bloomberg Television on Thursday that “every meeting is a live meeting” in times of uncertainty.
Economists in Bloomberg’s poll predict rates will stay at 2.75% until December 2027, when the ECB will start lowering them.

items.title: AI Panic Needs Some Nuclear Metaphors
body: Much about the global AI panic — could it really “kill us all by the end of the decade”? — is genuinely new, and thus extra-scary. Then again, the specter of human-engineered extinction is hardly novel; we have about eight decades of experience in thinking about it.
So what metaphors and lessons can we draw from the field of nuclear weapons as we wrap our minds around what lies ahead in artificial intelligence?

One of the oldest metaphors came from J. Robert Oppenheimer, sometimes called “the father of the atomic bomb.” Writing in 1953, when Washington and Moscow were already able to annihilate one another while irradiating the world, he likened America and the Soviet Union “to two scorpions in a bottle, each capable of killing the other, but only at the risk of his own life.”

In game theory, which was then in its heyday, Oppenheimer’s analogy was often paired with the Prisoner’s Dilemma, which analyzes the incentives for cooperation or betrayal between two people who are arrested and separately interrogated. Its upshot is that cooperation would be better for both, if they could trust each other; but since they can’t, defection may be the more rational choice.

These scorpions, or prisoners, bear a passing resemblance to contestants in today’s AI revolution, whether they’re companies (OpenAI and Anthropic, say) or the two AI superpowers, the United States and China.

Yes, it would be safer, for them and all of humanity, if, as Anthropic’s boss urges, the rivals start cooperating by “pacing the frontier” — voluntarily slowing down to give regulators time to catch up. But each must assume the other could cheat, so it may be safer to keep racing, even if that leads to dead scorpions or miserable prisoners.

“Whoever wins AI wins,” US President Donald Trump has said, believing that the US is ahead by a nose and seeing no reason to slow down. Beijing, as long as it’s slightly behind, sees no way to ease off without losing. So both hurtle forward.

Believe it or not, Oppenheimer’s metaphor may nonetheless be too optimistic — or not pessimistic enough — to fit today’s context. When rational players go round after round (as opposed to just once) in the Prisoner’s Dilemma, they can reach stability. That’s what happened during the Cold War in the form of deterrence.

But as leading AI scholars have been making clear all week, nothing about AI, which has advanced by leaps and bounds just in a few months, is stable. A more apt metaphor may be the one used by Thomas Schelling, a titan of nuclear strategy and winner of the Nobel Prize for his work in game theory.

As the Cold War advanced, Schelling imagined a situation in which two adversaries find themselves “in a room full of gasoline,” each holding matches. Neither can credibly threaten to strike his match, since the conflagration would kill them both. But each can, through provocation or miscalculation, raise the risk of incineration by inadvertent escalation or accident.

Schelling was describing a situation of brinkmanship that is captured in game theory with Chicken, a scenario in which two drivers race toward each other. If one swerves, the other wins. If both swerve, neither wins, but both are safe. If neither swerves, they crash. Translated to today’s AI situation, it looks as follows.

Whereas the Prisoner’s Dilemma allows for rationality (even for scorpions, in this mixed metaphor), Chicken describes something more frightening: the loss of control and, in Schelling’s phrase, a “threat that leaves something to chance.”

That seems to describe the AI race, as companies in the US, and presumably China, are creating large-language models and other agents that autonomously manipulate or attack other systems and have already done so.

As if that weren’t scary enough, the industry has also entered the phase of “recursive self-improvement,” as AI agents autonomously build the next generation of even more powerful models. It’s as though, in a gasoline-filled room, the matches were not only making sparks all by themselves but also building new matches, and then sophisticated flame throwers.

This makes one more metaphor relevant: the sword of Damocles. It was used by President John F. Kennedy in a speech at the United Nations. “Every inhabitant of this planet must contemplate the day when this planet may no longer be habitable,” he said; “every man, woman and child lives under a nuclear sword of Damocles, hanging by the slenderest of threads, capable of being cut at any moment by accident or miscalculation or by madness.”

That madness resembles visions I’ve had in the past week of AI agents going rogue. If Oppenheimer’s scorpions make us think of retaliation and Schelling’s gasoline-filled room evokes uncontrollable risk, the Damocles sword sums up the panic by positing extinction not for the individual players, but for the species.

The sword of Damocles allows for hope as well as despair. Hope, because in the years after Kennedy’s exhortation the world achieved a form of détente, with treaties for non-proliferation and arms control (an era that is now sadly turning into one of rearmament again). Today, that would mean collective pacing, plus mutual verification, as well as coordinated regulation by Washington, Beijing and others.

Better yet, the US and China could start playing a different game, called Stag Hunt. It imagines two hunters who must decide whether to cooperate and kill a stag that would feed both of them for a long time. If either defects, the other catches nothing, while the defector only gets a rabbit.

In today’s context, the stag represents the huge benefits that AI could bring to humanity, from curing its diseases to fixing its other problems. The upside of nuclear technology was mainly electricity generation; the bonus of superintelligence could be much larger.

What fills me with awe is the point at which the metaphors and game theory of the Cold War era break down. The scorpions, prisoners, car racers and other characters in our thought exercises all represented humans with agency interacting with an exogenous technology, namely fission. But what happens when the AI models themselves become players?

AI doesn’t share, at least not intrinsically, our human instinct to avoid catastrophe — a difference euphemistically called the “alignment problem.” That one insight is enough to explain why it’s imperative, as the jargon has it, always to keep a human in the loop, and to go no faster than human speed. This too is a lesson already learned by leaders during the late Cold War: An out-of-control AI contest, like a nuclear war, cannot be won, and must never be fought.

items.title: Austria's Plansee Is Challenging China's Critical Minerals Grip on Tungsten
body: Nestled between a turquoise-colored lake and the soaring peaks of the Austrian Alps, Plansee Group is building one of the West’s most formidable critical minerals operations outside China.

The closely held company, based in the town of Reutte, sells tungsten, a metal that attracts far less attention than rare earths but is no less vital to modern industry. The material’s exceptional hardness makes it ideal for tools that cut and shape car parts. Its resistance to heat is crucial to semiconductor manufacturing. And its extraordinary density, nearly twice that of lead, gives armor-piercing ammunition much of its penetrating power.

Few metals can match that versatility, but sourcing it comes with a familiar vulnerability: Beijing dominates the supply chain. A series of moves by China over the past two years — restricting exports, drawing in more raw material and, most recently, cutting off key shipments to Japan — has intensified a global scramble for tungsten. In turn, its cost has soared.

That marks a stark turnaround after years of low prices forced many Western tungsten suppliers out of business. A similar shift is playing out across several critical minerals markets, as Chinese export controls and surging prices put a spotlight on the handful of alternative producers capable of quickly boosting supply.

Plansee is one of them. The company has built up its position in tungsten over decades, securing ore from a mine in South Korea and expanding US processing alongside its European operations. Today, it’s by far the largest manufacturer outside China, accounting for about 12% of global demand and supplying some of the world’s most valuable companies, including ASML Holding NV and SpaceX.

Increasingly, the company’s advantage is that much of its tungsten requires no new mining at all. More than 90% of the 15,000 metric tons it can produce each year comes from worn drill bits, milling inserts and other scrap, thanks to two decades spent developing ways to recycle used material into tungsten comparable in quality to that made from ore.
“Our starting point was China independence,” Chairman Karlheinz Wex said from the company’s headquarters, located a two-hour drive south of Munich. “The basis for becoming independent was recycling.”

That strategy gives Plansee greater control over its materials — and more leverage as competition for supply intensifies. China still accounts for more than 80% of mined tungsten, while its own supplies are tightening as mines age and domestic demand grows. After the country became a net importer last year, Chinese buyers began aggressively snapping up US scrap, in some cases outbidding domestic traders, according to Wex.
China also curbed exports of intermediate tungsten products. Wex estimates that about 20,000 tons of material that flowed annually to Western markets a decade ago has since disappeared.
Amid supply concerns, the Trump administration effectively halted US tungsten scrap exports in August, requiring sellers to offer all of it to domestic buyers.

Tungsten is a niche market on paper, valued at only around $16 billion globally — about 5% of copper’s. But its reach is far greater. Carbide tools made with the metal are used throughout modern manufacturing, from aircraft and automobiles to computers and phones.
“The world would stand still without these carbide tools,” said Simon Jost, managing director of Plansee’s Ceratizit unit in Reutte.

Inside the highly-automated factory, robots navigate between hundreds of workers. They’re ferrying tungsten plates and rods to be stamped, pressed and polished. Some are as thin as a human hair and used by hospitals to perform surgeries. Others look like menacing claws and can bore tunnels through mountains. Nearly every manufactured product requires something to be drilled, cut or shaped along the way, Jost said.

Tungsten is hardly an isolated case of China’s dominance in critical minerals. The country is the leading refiner of the vast majority of strategic metals, according to the International Energy Agency. The IEA estimates that China’s rare earth export curbs alone could put $6.5 trillion in annual downstream production at risk. Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, warned this week about “dangerous dependencies” on Beijing for critical minerals.

Austria central bank Governor  Martin Kocher said policymakers are paying closer attention to how shortages of critical materials can constrain production and fuel inflation. Central bankers have long factored oil and gas into their models. Now they’re looking at less visible inputs such as tungsten, where a shortage of a relatively cheap material can hold up production worth many times more.

Plansee has treated the squeeze as an opportunity to gain market share and advertise its services. The company’s global network makes it one of the few able to turn scrap and ore into usable tungsten without relying on China. Material collected in Europe can be processed in Austria, Finland or Pennsylvania before moving to factories and customers.
Recycling leaves Plansee less exposed to volatile mining markets and swings in Chinese exports. The company is a rarity in Europe.

“We are not particularly good at recycling in Europe right now,” said Román Arjona, chief economist at the European Commission’s internal-market and industry directorate. Too much critical material is still lost because Europe lacks the investment, skills and infrastructure to recover it, he said.

Recycling also cuts Plansee’s environmental footprint. Products made from recycled tungsten generate four to five times fewer carbon emissions than those made from newly mined material, Wex said. Renewable sources provide 98% of Plansee’s electricity, helping the group cut its carbon footprint by almost a third over the past five years.
Revenue rose 4% to €2.35 billion in fiscal 2026, and Plansee has invested €145 million in new capacity to process concentrate, make powder and produce higher-value tungsten products.

Plansee’s location explains some of its success. Jewish chemist and entrepreneur Paul Schwarzkopf founded the company in the Alpine town of Reutte in 1921, lured from Berlin by cheap hydropower from nearby Lake Plansee.

Schwarzkopf fled to the US as Nazi persecution intensified, and his factory was expropriated and converted into an armaments plant. He returned after World War II and eventually recovered ownership following a prolonged restitution struggle. A century later, the same access to low-carbon power remains a competitive strength.

Plansee’s ability to produce tungsten outside China is becoming more valuable for the US, in particular. This year, the company formed a joint venture with Manhattan Five Partners — a US property developer that works with the federal government — to build a strategic reserve of tungsten oxide. Plansee plans to expand its Pennsylvania plant to process about 12,000 tons annually, using recycled scrap and ore from approved sources.

The push is becoming more urgent ahead of January 2027, when new Pentagon restrictions will further limit the use of tungsten originating in China, Russia, Iran or North Korea. Defense suppliers will increasingly need to trace the metal back to where it was mined or recycled and processed — playing to Plansee’s decades of investment in tracking material across borders.

Plansee is also locking in new supplies. It recently extended a deal to buy tungsten concentrate for another 21 years from   Almonty Industries Inc.’s Sangdong mine in South Korea. Plansee owns about 10% of Almonty, its largest shareholder, which is also restarting the long-shuttered Los Santos mine in Spain.

Sangdong is instructive of how tough it is to compete with China. The mine closed about three decades ago after cheap Chinese tungsten drove down prices. Now being revived, it could eventually supply as much as 20% of the tungsten concentrate produced outside China, according to Plansee.
This time, the deal includes protections designed to keep Sangdong viable if prices fall again.
“You must think long term,” Wex said.

The European Union is trying to build resilience more broadly. Its Critical Raw Materials Act calls for the bloc by 2030 to extract 10%, process 40% and recycle 25% of the strategic materials it consumes, while reducing dependence on any single foreign country.

Tungsten illustrates the challenge. Europe has mines, processors such as Plansee and a vast stock of the metal already embedded in tools and machinery. Almonty has been working to start up a major potential project in Spain since 2013, but the future of the operation has been thrown into doubt after a regional government issued a non-binding negative environmental assessment against it in July.
Ultimately, recycling more tungsten is key to reducing reliance on China — but only if the scrap remains in Europe long enough to be recovered.
“We need to make sure that all the used tools stay in the Western world,” Jost said.

items.title: King Charles Has a Perfect AI Watchdog for OpenAI and Anthropic
body: King Charles met with executives from the world’s top artificial intelligence companies this week, just as they were calling for government help in regulating their risky, frontier systems. The king should point to a source of help in his own backyard.

The UK’s AI Security Institute is the world’s best-funded agency for testing cutting-edge AI models, thanks to the £240 million ($325 million) it got from the British government in 2025, and an annual budget of about £66 million. The equivalent US agency in Washington, known as the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, gets just $10 million a year.

AISI is about three years old and has more than 100 technical staff who’ve come from AI safety organizations and academia, as well as tech companies including OpenAI, Anthropic PBC and Google DeepMind, many of them taking a pay cut to join the taxpayer-funded program. Agency workers are bound by strict non-disclosure agreements, but behind closed doors they talk of their concerns about the safety of novel AI systems, the same worry that compelled former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon and other engineers to speak out this month. Many also want to see more government intervention in the technology.

The leaders of AI firms say they want that too, but their warnings are falling on deaf ears in Washington. President Donald Trump is meeting Chinese leader Xi Jinping next week and Nvidia boss Jensen Huang is expected to attend a state dinner, but don’t expect a fruitful discussion about safety. Trump recently said fears about AI’s risks were a hoax and dismissed calls for a slowdown which could let China gain ground. Huang agreed this week, telling Trump, “We’re not going to let that happen, sir.”

But the “hoax” isn’t going away. The latest evidence comes from OpenAI, which says its AI models have misbehaved in several concerning ways, namely fabricating data and trying to bypass network restrictions. The company wants to report these incidents to the US federal government, and said it would propose a mechanism to do so.OpenAI said in its blog post: "We also believe that serious safety, security and misalignment incidents should be shared with the US federal government, and we are working to propose reporting mechanisms."

How often do companies ask for more government rules and get refused? Rarely. But specific recommendations like OpenAI’s on reporting are sensible and might just be palatable to the White House. There’s also a good chance AI companies will agree to embed independent evaluators to ensure models are being developed safely. That was a recent suggestion from Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei.
Those testers would play a vital role not only in scrutinizing risky new innovations but in allaying widespread fears as tech firms race to find the next big breakthrough.

Models such as ChatGPT initially improved thanks to so-called scaling laws — the notion that more computing power plus more data leads to smarter models. But the gains are becoming more expensive and incremental, leading engineering teams to pursue novel methods like recursive self-improvement, where AI systems help develop their own successors. That was the technique singled out by Coxon in an X post viewed more than 170 million times since Sept. 9, when he accused Anthropic and OpenAI of acting irresponsibly and “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”OpenAI and Anthropic do hire their own safety auditors, bound by company’s own commercial imperative of course. OpenAI recently posted a job ad for its “preparedness safety team” which offered a pay package of between $295,000 and $445,000 to “support preparations for recursive self-improvement." The company said it was “important that people in this role are tasteful and strategic.”
While the risks can be debated, his warning unquestionably shook public confidence. That alone calls for credible safety evaluations, and makes the identity of the evaluator matter immensely.

Britain’s AISI already has a track record of testing the latest AI systems. It got early access to Mythos, the Anthropic model that was initially restricted because of its cyber capabilities. The government-backed agency lacks a commercial conflict of interest, and its base in London gives it meaningful distance from the financial and ideological bubble of Silicon Valley.
“Our view is there should be a diverse range [of evaluators],” Mustafa Suleyman, the CEO of Microsoft AI, tells me. “AISI would be a good candidate.”

There are indeed other evaluation groups to choose from. Amodei recommends METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research), the Berkeley, California-based research firm, but there are questions about its independence. Having a government agency as an assessor would create a clearer route from testing to enforcement. AISI itself doesn’t have policing power today, and its relationships with AI labs are voluntary. It makes sense to give the agency more teeth. After all, what’s the point of monitoring dangerous new technology if you can’t stop it from being built?
Some of the most important regulators of high-risk technology are government backed, from the International Atomic Energy Agency based in Vienna to the Federal Aviation Administration in Washington.
The same principle should apply to AI. Altman and Amodei may have their own ideas about who should oversee their work, but in the spirit of proper oversight, the choice shouldn’t be entirely theirs.

It would be a great irony if meeting King Charles, a symbol of Britain’s former empire, helped encourage today’s American tech royalty to think about empowering a sophisticated AI inspector in London. But it would be prudent to do so. The UK has already built the watchdog they say they want. The next step is inviting it in and giving it some real authority.

items.title: Greek Bank Rally to Get Fresh Impetus as Stocks Rejoin Top Index
body: Greek bank stocks are set for another boost after staging a remarkable recovery since the country’s sovereign debt crisis, with the four biggest lenders rejoining Europe’s top benchmark on Monday.

National Bank of Greece SA, Eurobank SA, Piraeus Bank SA and Alpha Bank SA will reenter the Stoxx Europe 600 Index next week, when the index provider’s reclassification of Greece as a developed market takes effect. Stoxx’s upgrade comes about ten years after Greece was cut to emerging status, and will open the door to a new wave of investors, including passive funds that track major indexes and active managers who are restricted to developed markets.

The sector has had a stellar recovery since the crisis. The stock market shut for five weeks in 2015 as capital controls gripped the country, with shares of Greek banks plunging 94%. Greece has subsequently turned its economy around, regaining investment grade status with all major ratings firms. The FTSE ATHEX Banks Index is up more than 400% over the past ten years.

“Slowly but steadily Greece moved from crisis to growth and it is not a restructuring story anymore,” said Eglé Fredriksson, a portfolio manager at East Capital Group. “Similar valuations and faster growth is actually an attractive profile for Greece versus developed Europe.”
Read more: Greek Stocks Crown Comeback With Promotion to Europe’s Top Index

Investor Joe Faraday, head of European equities at Baillie Gifford, particularly likes Piraeus for its rapid growth in corporate lending and fee income. “Years spent fighting for survival have created a performance culture that is rare in banking and that is now being paired with a much healthier Greek economy.”

Greek banks have also outperformed most European peers this year, with shares in the top four lenders all up more than 30%. That compares with a 22% gain for the Euro Stoxx Banks Index they are set to join.

“Greece offers one of Europe’s most attractive banking markets, supported by investment-led GDP growth, and some of the highest lending growth in Europe,” Jefferies analysts including Alexander Demetriou wrote in a note this month. Greece’s GDP is forecast to grow 1.9% in 2026, outpacing the European Union’s 1.2% growth, according to Bloomberg consensus estimates.

Those fundamentals have already drawn investor attention, but inclusion in the Stoxx 600 Index will also pull passive money into the stocks. The four banks combined are estimated to see inflows of about $2.2 billion, according to strategists at JPMorgan Chase & Co.

Despite the sector rally, Greek bank stocks remain among the cheapest lenders in Europe. Their average price-to-book ratio of 1.3 times is more than 20% below that of Italian peers and nearly 30% below Spanish lenders, according to Bloomberg Intelligence.
The sector’s recovery is being reflected in analyst ratings, with the four Greek lenders all having overwhelmingly positive recommendations among analysts tracked by Bloomberg.

Deutsche Bank analyst Alfredo Alonso rates all of the banks a buy, noting strong second-quarter results and upgrades to guidance for some of the lenders. “The sector offers clear earnings visibility that, in our view, remains undervalued, especially considering higher growth ahead than many European counterparts,” Alonso wrote in a note this month.

To be sure, it may not all be smooth sailing. Morgan Stanley strategists and economists including Matthew Nguyen and Chiara Zangarelli wrote in a recent report that the “balance of risks becomes less one-way into early 2027, as the index-upgrade trade matures and a spring election brings political outlook into focus.”

The outcome of next year’s election is far from certain at the moment. Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis’ center-right New Democracy party has a comfortable lead in polls, but it is also seen falling short of the share of the vote needed to form a one-party government, as Greeks struggle with a cost of living crisis and a decline in living standards.

Still, the bank stocks have another market-related catalyst ahead, with index compiler MSCI set to formally upgrade Greece from emerging to developed market status in May 2027, an event that Morgan Stanley said is “a more important benchmark event for long-only European investors” than the Stoxx upgrade.

Five other Greek stocks are also set to join the Stoxx Europe 600 on Monday, including Metlen Energy & Metals Plc, Public Power Corp SA, GEK Terna SA, Motor Oil Hellas Corinth Refineries SA and Jumbo SA.

items.title: Andy Burnham's Right Where He Didn't Want to Be: 'In Hock' to Bond Markets
body: After the early optimism of Andy Burnham’s premiership, the UK’s new prime minister now finds himself right where he didn’t want to be: at the mercy of bond markets.

Burnham’s plans for a low-key, don’t-rock-the-boat budget on Oct. 28 that would sustain the administration’s momentum in the polls is careening into higher UK borrowing costs, with economists estimating Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey will need to find £10 billion ($13.5 billion) to stabilize public finances, either by cutting spending or raising tax.

A decision from the Bank of England to slow how quickly it’s offloading its bond portfolio, effectively reducing the supply of gilts, gave yields some much-needed relief on Thursday. But the effects of the war in Iran on energy prices means borrowing costs are still substantially higher than where they were when Burnham took office two months ago.

All that means the budget is shaping up to be a harsh inflection point for Burnham and Healey, where the upbeat rhetoric that’s helped Labour register a bounce in voter opinion will have to confront Britain’s fragile economic position. While Healey’s main constituency may be the electorate, his package entails the possibility of a move to placate investors at a time when the interest paid on government borrowing is high enough to account for 10% of its spending.
“The budget is the big reckoning,” said Tom Pope, chief economist at the Institute for Government, a think tank. “The politics is hard because Burnham and Healey haven’t prepared the ground.”

Burnham appeared to take his first steps toward doing that on Wednesday, when he said the budget “is going to be challenging, because the picture around the world is challenging.” Those words marked an abrupt shift in tone for the new prime minister, who pledged on his first day in office that his administration would “bring back hope.”

It’s almost a year since Burnham broke cover in his attempts to supplant Keir Starmer. His first major intervention on that journey involved an interview where he told the New Statesman magazine, “we’ve got to get beyond this thing of being in hock to the bond markets.” The then-mayor of Manchester said he was criticizing Britain’s “low growth doom loop,” which he wanted to escape with his plan to reshape the UK economy. And yet, until that bears fruit, in office he now has to respond to those same financial forces.

What happens in markets in the next fortnight will be crucial for Healey. That’s because the Office for Budget Responsibility, which produces the economic forecasts that underpin the budget, will use a market average for key financial indicators like gilt yields from readings taken over the period.

As it stands, with the 10-year gilt yield at 5.22% on Thursday — compared to the 4.8% assumed by the OBR at the time of the last budget — Healey is estimated to have lost about half of the £23.6 billion fiscal buffer he inherited from former chancellor Rachel Reeves, according to Bloomberg Economics. That’s because higher borrowing costs mean higher debt interest payments, which constrain Healey via the government’s main fiscal rule that requires day-to-day spending to be covered by tax receipts by the end of the Parliament.

The Resolution Foundation, an influential think tank in Labour circles, estimates Healey has as little as £5 billion of fiscal headroom, when setting the increase in borrowing costs alongside other spending commitments Burnham’s announced, like his pledge to end rough sleeping and a commitment to plug a £4.7 billion hole in the government’s defense investment plan.

“Positive vibes can’t hide the painful policy trade-offs facing the chancellor,” said Sophie Hale, research director at the Resolution Foundation. Measures “to repair vital fiscal buffers” will be needed she said.

The worsening financial conditions come at a time when some critics of the government’s economic strategy are becoming more vocal. Andy Haldane, the former chief economist of the Bank of England and an unofficial adviser to Burnham as he prepared for power, told LBC Radio on Monday that markets now “suspect that this is a traditional tax-and-spend socialist government with better TikTok videos.”

Jim O’Neill, the former Goldman Sachs chief economist who also informally advised Burnham before he took office, has warned Healey against lifting taxes on businesses, saying it would risk hurting economic growth.

Those warnings come as some in the City of London were underwhelmed by their first major engagement with Healey in his new role, which offered little this week beyond the chance to stroll around Number 10 Downing Street and hear a brief speech from a chancellor preoccupied with the spike in household energy costs.
“We in government will provide the fiscal discipline and stability,” Healey told the reception of business leaders. “Together we can write the next chapter of Britain’s growth story.”

Burnham has delayed a planned investment summit that was due to take place in London to next year, with the event now set to be held outside of the UK capital, according to a person familiar with the matter. The decision to delay the summit was first reported by Sky News.

Healey’s budget preparations also suffered a setback on the news that hedge fund founder Chris Rokos, one of Britain’s top taxpayers, is set to leave the UK, putting fresh scrutiny on whether Labour is doing enough to attract and retain wealthy residents, or whether further departures are in the offing as anxiety builds over potential budget tax rises.

Sensing the government’s vulnerability on the issue, Andrew Griffith, the main opposition Conservative Party’s newly-appointed shadow chancellor, used his first major speech on Thursday to challenge the government to rule out higher taxes.

Options Healey is considering to raise revenue at the budget include higher levies on banks, oil and gas companies, and gambling firms, along with increases to the tax on capital gains, according to people familiar with the matter. Meanwhile he is looking for departmental savings to close the £4.7 billion gap in Britain’s defense investment plan.
“They’re in a very difficult position,” said Al Cattermole, fixed-income portfolio manager at Mirabaud Asset Management. “The market is very nervous.”

items.title: 'King CATL' Stranglehold on Chinese EV Makers Starts Loosening
body: Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. has long dominated the global market for electric-vehicle batteries. Now some of its customers in China are trying to break free.

Automakers including Li Auto Inc. and Xiaomi Corp. have started to design their own cells and are adding new suppliers including Sunwoda Electronic Co. The moves have sparked concerns that a larger trend of “de-CATLization” is behind the company’s recent $100 billion market rout.

The carmakers are trying to “enhance their bargaining power” because they’re squeezed by components inflation, said Morgan Stanley analyst Tim Hsiao. “It’s a good idea and makes commercial sense to diversify.”

The push reflects the tensions between large suppliers and their customers in the world’s largest auto market, where fierce pricing competition is weighing on carmaker margins. Profits at CATL, however, have continued to grow in large part because of its outsized market dominance and pricing power.

“CATL takes all the profits, squeezing downstream automakers,” Hu Xijin, former editor-in-chief of China’s nationalist tabloid Global Times, wrote in a Weibo post this week. “There’s a saying circulating in the industry: the world has suffered under King CATL for too long.”
CATL didnt’ immediately respond to a request for comment. The company’s shares declined 0.9% in Shenzhen. They’re down 17% this year.
Read More: CATL Shares Drop 10% in Two Days as Outlook Worries Mount

Li Auto has been at the forefront of the diversification push and plans to gradually supply all of its models with self-developed batteries, it said on Sept. 7. Earlier this year, the company’s new i6 electric sedan was delayed when CATL didn’t deliver batteries on time. Li Auto had to tap alternative supplier Sunwoda to ease the bottleneck.

Xiaomi, which has long relied on batteries from CATL and BYD Co., earlier this month unveiled a new battery platform designed with two smaller producers, CALB Group Co. and Sunwoda. Called Longjia, it’s slated to go into Xiaomi’s new line of Skynomad sport utility vehicles.
With the development of autonomous driving, carmakers have also begun to focus more on developing energy systems and battery expertise in house, said Hsiao, the Morgan Stanley analyst.

“So, on one hand, it’s driven by business strategy, while on the other hand, power solutions remain very important for their future development — not only for vehicles but also for embodied AI,” he said.

items.title: Chinese Robotics Suppliers Rise on Tesla Optimus Audit Report
body: Shares of Chinese robotics‑component suppliers climbed after a local report said Tesla Inc. teams had arrived in the country to audit suppliers and place additional orders to boost production of its Optimus humanoid model.

The Solactive China Humanoid Robotics Index, which tracks companies in the sector, jumped as much as 2.4% following the report by 21st Century Business Herald. Shares of actuator maker Ningbo Tuopu Group, which rose as much as 7%, contributed the most to the index’s gain. Sensor manufacturer Ningbo Joyson Electronic Corp. and thermal-management supplier Zhejiang Sanhua Intelligent Controls Co. both advanced by more than 4%.

The stock moves highlight the key role of Chinese suppliers in robotics development worldwide. Optimism around humanoid robots has emerged as an important theme in China’s market this year, driving gains in automation and precision‑manufacturing shares.

“Tesla’s reported supplier audits are a positive commercialization signal for China’s humanoid supply chain, pointing to progress toward repeatable Optimus production,” Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Ian Ma said. “Near-term sentiment could stay supported if audits lead to confirmed supplier nominations and larger orders.”

Tesla’s teams arrived in the city of Ningbo this week for audits focused on production consistency and exclusivity requirements, the local report said, citing unnamed supply-chain sources. The US tech company, chaired by billionaire Elon Musk, has already begun placing orders from suppliers tied to the Optimus robot, the report said.
Tesla didn’t immediately respond to a Bloomberg request for comment.
While accelerating production of Optimus may lift suppliers’ near‑term outlook, Ma said earnings impact across the supply chain is likely to stay modest until robot volumes scale up.
In July, Musk said 2026 will be a ‘massive’ capex year, with plans to spend more than $25 billion and significantly expand factory operations, including the production of Optimus robots.

items.title: China Urges Stable Coal Output as Prices Rise to Three-Year High
body: China’s government urged coal miners to ensure stable production and supply after spot prices for the power-station fuel rallied to the highest level in nearly three years.

The National Development and Reform Commission, National Energy Administration, and National Mine Safety Administration recently issued a joint notice calling on coal-producing regions and companies to accelerate efforts to ensure steady output and promote the reopening of mines to support economic growth and energy supply, the NEA said in a post on its WeChat account.

Chinese coal output has fallen after a deadly accident in Shanxi province in May prompted a series of safety inspections. Coking coal for steel-making initially felt the biggest impact, with futures rising to a two-year high in early September.

Spot prices for thermal, or power-station, coal have recently surged as electricity generators stock up on supplies before a busy holiday period in the country with the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day occurring within days of each other. Prices at the hub of Qinhuangdao rose 1.9% this week to 980 yuan ($146), the highest level since October 2023.

items.title: AirAsia's Fernandes Hits Back at Critics as Stock Slumps
body: A defiant AirAsia Group Bhd. co-founder Tony Fernandes said reports Malaysia’s government has asked rivals for help were false, saying the low-cost airline will emerge from its current crisis stronger than before.

The airline’s woes have mounted this year following the outbreak of war in the Middle East, which sent oil and jet fuel prices surging. Its stock has plunged around 75% — since the conflict started amid concern the carrier is under growing financial strain. The carrier has taken the unusual step of offloading six newly-delivered planes, including two in July, Bloomberg News reported earlier.
“We’ve been through many many crises, but we’ve always come out stronger,” Fernandes said at a briefing Friday in Bangkok. “Covid was far, far worse than what we are dealing with now.”

The hastily arranged briefing came after AirAsia’s stock slumped 21% to a four-year low on Thursday after reports Malaysia’s government had asked other local airlines to potentially absorb the cash-strapped carrier’s domestic market share.

“I can say confidently the government said we never said anything like that,” Fernandes said. “You cannot just say, “Oh, this airline is going to take AirAsia’s capacity.” I mean, it’s the most ludicrous statement I have seen in 25 years.”
AirAsia had 954 million ringgit ($233 million) in cash and equivalents as of the end of June, one of the lowest balances among airlines tracked by Bloomberg globally.
“I have better things to do right now than have this press conference” because of an inaccurate article, he said. “We are good at managing cash and we are strong in liquidity,” he added.
“Things get blown out of proportion when it’s AirAsia,” Fernandes said. “I sneeze, it’s a big story.”

items.title: BOJ Split Vote Sends Bearish Signal on Yen, Strategists Say
body: The yen dropped after the Bank of Japan’s decision to hike rates as a split vote sent bearish signals, strategists said. The Japanese currency fell as much as 0.8% and bond markets erased earlier gains after the central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point to 1.25%.

Board members voted 7-2 to raise the key rate in a move was predicted by all economists surveyed by Bloomberg. Investor focus now shifts to Governor Kazuo Ueda’s post-decision press conference scheduled for 3:30 p.m. Tokyo time.

items.title: Flooding Kills Three People as Heavy Rains Hit Northern Vietnam
body: Heavy rains triggered flooding and landslides across northern Vietnam, killing three people and damaging thousands of homes as well as more than 22,000 hectares of crops.

The northern region has experienced downpours since Sept. 14, with some areas receiving as much as 653 millimeters of rain, according to a statement on the government’s website. More than 16,000 of houses have been inundated while rice and other crops have been damaged.

National and provincial roads have been affected by 11 landslides and flooding in 30 locations, causing traffic tie-ups. The Hanoi-Ho Chi Minh City railway was flooded to a depth of about one meter. Several train services on the north-south railway were suspended Thursday and Friday.
In the northern coastal province of Thanh Hoa, more than 29,000 officials and soldiers were mobilized for emergency assistance.

Some Hanoi schools switched to online classes or gave students the day off Thursday as streets inundated with as much as one-meter of floodwaters caused gridlocked in the center of the capital city, state media reported. More heavy rain is expected from Thanh Hoa province to the city of Hue through the weekend, with some areas forecast to receive a deluge of over 100 millimeters.

Vietnam’s long coastline makes it vulnerable to storms roaring in from the South China Sea, while climate change and deforestation have increased the country’s potential for severe damage. As many as five more storms are expected off the coast the rest of the year, with one or two possibly sweeping over Vietnam’s mainland.

Natural disasters have killed or left 63 people missing in Vietnam in 2026, causing total losses of around 2.2 trillion dong ($84.6 million). Financial losses are down 84.9% from the same period last year when the country was hit by severe typhoons and flooding, according to separate government statement.

Meanwhile, El Nino is expected to reduce rainfall in central and southern Vietnam by 10% to 50% later this year, potentially affecting around 350,000 hectares of rice in the Mekong Delta. Severe water shortages are also forecast in the central highlands, the country’s largest coffee growing region.

items.title: Yen Extends Declines After BOJ Hikes Rates With Two Dissents
body: The yen extended its drop against the dollar after the Bank of Japan lifted interest rates as expected, with two dissents casting doubts on the outlook for further policy tightening.

Japan’s currency fell as much as 0.7% to 157.09 per greenback, while Japanese government bonds erased earlier gains. While the move was predicted by all economists surveyed by Bloomberg, the vote was 7-2 as board members Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato dissented.
Read more: BOJ Hikes Rates at Fastest Pace Since 1990 After Bessent’s Calls

The outcome was “not hawkish enough for markets and should push USDJPY higher and front-end JPY yields lower,” said Chidu Narayanan, chief APAC strategist at Wells Fargo. “Two dissents at this meeting, albeit from the two most dovish members of the board, does not support market expectations of a slew of rapid rates hikes from the BOJ.”

Japan’s Nikkei 225 extended gains to as much as 2% in afternoon trading as the yen weakened. The Topix index was little changed as financial shares weighed on the broader gauge. Spillover in other currency and bond markets was also limited.

The BOJ’s rate increase came after the Federal Reserve’s hawkish hike earlier this week pushed the yen weaker, partly reversing a sharp rally earlier this month fueled by expectations of faster BOJ tightening, an unwind of yen-funded carry trades and speculation that Japanese pension funds could shift more money to domestic assets.
Traders will focus on BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda’s post-decision press conference, which typically starts at 3:30 p.m. in Tokyo, for clues on the pace and scope of further tightening.

“I expect a neutral-to-slightly hawkish tone, emphasizing that every meeting remains ‘live’ from here given resilient growth, persistent inflation risks and a policy rate that remains accommodative even at 1.25%,” said Masahiko Loo, senior fixed income strategist at State Street Investment Management.

Strategists say dollar-yen could climb toward 160 if investors conclude the BOJ’s tightening path will struggle to keep pace with the Fed’s. The risk is particularly acute if subsequent communication from the BOJ is interpreted as dovish, given that a quarter-point increase had already been largely priced into markets.

The latest slide also puts intervention risk back in focus after Japan and the US carried out their first coordinated yen-buying operation this summer since 1998. Officials have emphasized the speed and disorderliness of currency moves rather than any specific level, but another push toward 160 could test their tolerance.
“We should expect further Japan-US intervention in forex markets if the yen is pressured again past 160 per dollar,” said Neil Newman, head of strategy at Astris Advisory Japan.

Japan spent a record ¥15.4 trillion ($98.3 billion) on intervention in the month through Aug. 26, according to Finance Ministry data. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has since continued to signal support for a stronger yen, potentially adding to traders’ reluctance to rebuild bearish positions.

items.title: Big Iron Ore Miners Deplete Reserves Faster Than They Replace
body: The world’s biggest iron ore producers are depleting ore reserves faster than they can replenish them, as the cost and complexity of developing replacements continues to rise, according to Wood Mackenzie Ltd.

The six largest iron ore producers, which includes BHP Group and Rio Tinto Group, collectively depleted 11.1 billion tons of ore reserves that could be sold between 2016 and 2025, the consultancy said in a report released Thursday. Only three replaced the volume they mined over the period, and some spent five times more than others to add new reserves, it found.

The industry is increasingly facing an issue with grade depletion, which occurs when the average iron ore content in a mine drops as it ages and requires operators to dig deeper and invest more to extract. Miners are now reaching a point where it’s no longer about growth, but keeping operations running.

“The main challenge for the current iron ore industry is rising costs to maintain existing production,” said Mihir Vora, Wood Mackenzie’s research director for metals and mining. “The industry is investing to sustain production, but it is having to work harder to stand still.”
Read More: The World’s Biggest Iron Ore Windfall Is Fading for Australia

Costs for major miners have roughly doubled for some companies since 2016, Wood Mackenzie said. Cash margins across the industry peaked in 2021 and have since settled at around $50-$60 a ton, shrinking the margin to absorb rising costs and falling prices.

The analysis also found ore grades had fallen by as much as 1.6 percentage points among some miners since 2016. Higher-grade material is increasingly required to offset the depletion of lower-grade ore, while impurity levels, including alumina, are rising in some products.

items.title: When War Damages Cultural Treasures, What Can UNESCO Do?
body: I don’t know if artificial intelligence poses an existential threat, but the human damage to civilization’s cultural legacy is a matter of record. It continues to this day with the violent erosion of our historical heritage through war.

This week, Saudi Arabia said it intercepted a drone attack on Mecca launched from Yemen by Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The Saudis said it was the second such attempt, citing a ballistic-missile launch nine years ago. The Houthis denied firing drones toward the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad; in 2017, they said they were targeting a military installation some 40 miles from the holy city.

In April, I wrote about the risks posed to the splendid 400-year-old Shah mosque in Isfahan by US and Israeli bombing of Iran’s nearby nuclear research hub. The historic edifice hasn’t suffered a direct hit, but blast waves from the assaults have shaken tiles loose and damaged windows. The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) has designated the mosque and nearly 1,000 other cultural monuments around the world as “so exceptional as to transcend national boundaries and to be of common importance for present and future generations of all humanity.” That hasn’t prevented desecration.

Last week, two UNESCO arms released a joint report about the damage inflicted on a 1,000-year-old Hindu clifftop temple during last year’s border dispute between Thailand and Cambodia. The agency suggested those responsible could face “criminal liability” — but the legal, evidentiary and regulatory hurdles to pursuing that route are laborious. Despite surviving centuries of depredation, these priceless relics rarely have the luxury of time.

At least two international courts have adjudicated on the Thai-Cambodia quarrel, recognizing the promontory hosting the ancient Preah Vihear temple as Cambodian. But they left open the question of who owns the surrounding territory, which sits directly on the frontier between the two nations. And so the fighting engulfed the entire area, including the temple. A photo published by UNESCO appears to show the collapse of the front of one ornamental gateway in the complex.

Criminal liability was also a potential recourse in 2024 after Israeli bombing in Lebanon came close to the 2,000-year-old Temple of Jupiter in Baalbek and the archaeological zones of Tyre, which include Roman baths and crusader fortifications. Instead, Lebanese officials requested — and eventually received — what’s called “enhanced protection” from UNESCO’s Committee for the Protection of Cultural Property in the Event of Armed Conflict. That adds an additional level of moral opprobrium to any attack that vandalizes the sites. Lebanon pledged that the locations wouldn’t be used for military purposes.

But ethical qualms aren’t enough to deter destruction, especially when non-state actors are involved. From 2015 to 2017, the terrorist group Islamic State demolished several temples in the ancient Syrian city of Palmyra. These included the Temple of BelThe name of the Palmyrene god Bel derives from the semitic word Baal (Lord) that was a generic name for the pagan rivals of the monotheistic deity of ancient Israel., which was dedicated in the year 32, arguably within the lifetime of Jesus of Nazareth. It predated the Colosseum in Rome. The battles that eventually retook the site from ISIS further despoiled Palmyra.

Criminal prosecutions may be easier if the antagonists are not nation states — and you can identify specific assailants. In 2012, Islamist fighters associated with Al-Qaeda smashed most of the historic mausoleums in the city of Timbuktu in Mali, some of which date to the 13th century. The episode produced the only conviction of any person for the war crime of heritage destruction: Ahmad Al Faqi Al Mahdi, the head of the Ansar Dine militia’s morality police during its 10-month occupation of the city. He was imprisoned first in the Netherlands and then in Scotland; his whereabouts since completing his sentence (nine years reduced to seven) are unknown.

Although a legal precedent was established, no comparable punishments have followed. In the meantime, the tombs — traditionally constructed of mud in the manner of the Great Mosque of Djenne to the south of Timbuktu — have been rebuilt.

Even if it falls short of providing protection in times of war, UNESCO’s list of heritage sites embodies our reverence for the past, appealing to primal instincts that are the opposite of carnage: preservation and remembrance.

Take the Dormition Cathedral in Kyiv. Built in the 11th century, it went through several alterations before suffering a catastrophic fire in the 18th century. Rebuilt shortly afterwards with baroque splendor, it was destroyed again in 1941 either by occupying Nazis or opposing resistance forces. It remained a ruin for six decades until Ukraine became independent following the collapse of the Soviet Union. The cathedral’s UNESCO-approved reconstruction was completed in 2000.
And then, on June 15, 2026, a Russian drone attack set the cathedral roof on fire and damaged the interior.

AI is trained on human knowledge and thus absorbs human foibles — but surely something of our nobler selves can also be incorporated. I can only hope that UNESCO’S records feed into the models and can influence computer-directed military operations to avoid attacking these communal treasures.

items.title: The $2.4 Billion Legacy Project Changing Belgrade
body: Every few weeks, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic visits the sprawling EXPO 2027 construction site just outside Belgrade to check on the $2.4 billion investment seen locally as his legacy project, and to update his social media followers on the progress.

As he stood by massive steel plinths in late July, trucks transported sand to and from the future pavilions of more than 140 countries. The event — the biggest of its kind in the Western Balkans since the wars that tore up former Yugoslavia three decades ago — will serve as an “engine that will drive development” from tourism and hospitality to construction, transport and trade, Vucic said in an Instagram video.

He has also said he hopes that it will help recast Serbia’s image. Action movie star Jackie Chan, Olympic gold medalist Usain Bolt, Chinese badminton champion Lin Dan, as well as Serbia’s own Jelena Jankovic, a former top-ranked tennis player, serve as brand ambassadors.

When the three-month-long exhibition – ‘Play for Humanity: Sport and Music for All’ – ends in August, the complex is slated to become a new suburb of the capital, with thousands of apartments, a rail link to the airport, and a dock on the Sava River. A sports stadium big enough to seat 52,000 people will be completed in 2028, ready to host the UEFA Europa League final a year later.

Vucic wants to see the project through to completion, but he and his ruling Progressive Party would need to win an election next month. He has called a snap parliamentary vote for Oct. 25 as he plans to step down as president and run for prime minister in a bid to extend his hold on power over the nation of 6.6 million people. Some polls indicate it’s a tight race that he may lose.

Vucic has dominated Serbia’s politics for more than a decade. During that time the country attracted more foreign investment than any other in the western Balkans as he balanced ties between the European Union, Russia, China and the US. The economy doubled to around $99.95 billion. But he’s facing mounting public discontent with his rule.

Over the past two years, student-led protests have grown into a mass movement that has now entered electoral politics. Its candidates promise to battle corruption, improve the rule of law and judicial independence, expand labor rights and ensure better access to health care and education.

Such tensions have made EXPO 2027 a lightning rod for political opponents, who see the event as a way for the ruling administration to siphon off public funds, while increasing public debt and widening the wealth gap between Belgrade and the provinces.

Five small opposition groups, including the People’s Movement of Serbia, have called on the Paris-based Bureau International des Expositions, which chose Belgrade, to cancel the exhibition. They also warned about “risks to the security and health” of participants, citing the concrete canopy collapse at a renovated train station in 2024 that killed 16 people.

Those worries surfaced in a European Parliament report on Serbia last year, which urged participants to “take into account the serious concerns and evidence of widespread corruption linked to the ruling authorities, as well as the reported lack of compliance with basic construction standards and legal requirements in the organization and construction.”
The authorities have dismissed the claims as politically motivated and baseless.

The 25 hectare- (62 acre-) exhibition site used to be farmland. Serbia is investing €1.23 billion ($1.4 billion) in its transformation into fairgrounds, and another €700 million in related infrastructure, according to EXPO 2027, the state company overseeing the preparations. Fees for the brand ambassadors haven’t been disclosed, and the organizers say the celebrities will be paid by unspecified sponsors.

Around 1.6 million visitors are expected at the event. The Belgrade-based Louis Berger Adria consultancy estimated it will generate more than €9 billion in new value for the economy by 2037 and €3.8 billion in tax revenues over 10 years. It said that every dinar of public investment may generate 1.91 dinars in tax revenue, along with boosting employment.
“It’s been an enormous challenge but the benefits are even bigger,” said EXPO 2027 director Danilo Jerinic in an interview.

Serbia has selected PowerChina as the main contractor, and has asked the Beijing-based company to add a thousand more laborers to ensure pavilions are ready by December, according to Jerinic. More than 4,000 people are already working in three shifts around the clock, he said.

After the exhibition, around 700 hectares of adjacent land will be offered to private companies, mainly real estate developers. Residents of this new area will have access to schools, retail and office space, as well as the Nikola Tesla airport rail link. And, by reinforcing the Sava River embankment with a port, a waterborne route to central Belgrade.

Such a carefully planned urban space would mark a break from practices of the past three decades, when authorities often turned a blind eye to structures built without permits or planning, leading to shanty town-style suburbs near cities, including the capital.
For Jerinic, “the EXPO will be an example of how to activate a completely new location in a city.”

items.title: Copper Set for Weekly Gain as Chinese Buyers Return to the Fore
body: Copper headed for a weekly gain, as signs of a rebound in Chinese demand helped to offset hawkish messaging from the Federal Reserve about the likelihood of more interest rate rises.

Benchmark futures were little changed near $14,460 a ton on the London Metal Exchange on Friday, on pace for the 11th weekly advance in the past 12. That streak saw the metal advance to a record earlier this month.

In China, the Yangshan premium — a gauge of demand named after the port in Shanghai that’s a major entry point for imported copper — rose to $121 a ton on Thursday, the highest level since November 2022. Meanwhile, domestic copper production fell slightly in August from the month before.

Copper has risen 16% this year as bets that the Trump administration would hit refined metal with tariffs triggered a surge of imports into the US, squeezing availability elsewhere. This week’s hike by the Fed — the first since 2023 — had little impact, even with hawkish messaging on the scope for further tightening. Higher rates typically damp demand for non-yielding assets like commodities.

“We expect base metals to remain mostly range-bound in the coming weeks, as supply-side risks offset a fragile macro backdrop,” analysts at BMI, a Fitch Solutions company, said in a note. “Markets continue to wait for a firm decision on US copper tariffs.”
Copper was 0.2% lower at $14,458.50 a ton on the LME at 10:57 a.m. in Singapore. Other metals were little changed, with aluminum declining 0.3%.
Iron ore added 0.8% to $97.15 a ton in Singapore, rising for a third day.
